The nunation in *yawma'idhin* (that day) is a replacement for the omitted genitive: that is, "the day of the coming of the Overwhelming." *Khāshiʿa* means humbled, abased. Anything that is subdued and still is called *khāshiʿ*. It is said: "the sound was humbled" when it became faint, and "he was humbled in his prayer" when he became submissive and lowered his head.

The word "faces" here refers to their owners.

Muqatil said: "It means the disbelievers, because they were arrogant toward worshipping Allah."

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: "Humbled in the Fire." It has also been said that it means the faces of the Jews and Christians specifically.

The first view is better.

His saying: *ʿāmila nāṣiba* (laboring, toiling). The meaning of *ʿāmila* is that they do laborious work.

The lexicographers said: "It is said of a man when he persists in his journey: '*ʿamila yaʿmalu ʿamalan*' (he labored, labors, labor), and it is said of a cloud when its lightning persists: 'it has labored, labors, labor.'"

Al-Shawkani's Fath al-Qadir, on surah 89, verses 1–5 (part 3 of 4):

It has been said that this work is dragging chains and shackles and wading through the Fire. *Nasibah* means weary (*ta'biyah*). It is said that *nasiba* (with the vowel *kasra*) *yansabu nasaban* means to become weary. The meaning is that in the Hereafter they will be weary because of what they encounter of the punishment of Allah.

It has also been said that His words "working, toiling" refer to this world, since there is no work in the Hereafter. That is, they work in this world in disbelief and sins, and they toil in that.

It has also been said that they work in this world and toil in the Hereafter. The first view is preferable.

Qatadah said: "﴿Working, toiling﴾: they were arrogant in this world toward obedience to Allah, so Allah made them work and made them toil in the Fire, by dragging heavy chains, carrying shackles, and standing barefoot and naked in the open plains, ﴿on a day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4]."

al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "They did not work for Allah in this world and did not toil, so Allah makes them work and toil in Jahannam."

al-Kalbi said: "They are dragged on their faces in the Fire."

He also said: "They are obliged to climb a mountain of iron in Jahannam, and they toil there at the utmost degree of toil, by handling chains and shackles and wading through the Fire, as camels wade through mud."

The majority of readers (qira'at) read ﴿working, toiling﴾ with *raf'* (nominative) in both words, as two further predicates of the subject, or with an implied subject of which these two are predicates. Ibn Muhaysin, 'Isa, Humayd, and Ibn Kathir in one narration from him read both with *nasb* (accusative), as circumstantial accusatives (*hal*) or as accusatives of dispraise (*dhamm*).

His words ﴿they will burn in a blazing Fire﴾ are another predicate of the subject. That is, they will enter a fire extremely intense in heat. It is said: "The day became hot" (*hamiya al-nahar*) and "the oven became hot" (*hamiya al-tannur*), meaning its heat intensified.

al-Kisa'i said: "It is said *ishtadda hamy al-nahar* and *hamwuhu* with the same meaning."

The majority read *tasla* with a *fatha* on the *ta'*, in the active voice. Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, and Abu Bakr read both with a *damma*, in the passive voice. Abu Ra'ja' read with a *damma* on the *ta'*, a *fatha* on the *sad*, and a shadda on the *lam*. The pronoun refers to the faces (*wujuh*) in all these readings, and what is meant is their owners, as previously mentioned. The pronoun is the same.

﴿They will be given drink from a boiling spring﴾. The "boiling spring" (*'ayn aniyah*) means one extremely hot. *Aniy* is that which has reached the end of its heat, from *al-iyna'*, meaning delay. It is said *anahu yu'nihi in'a'an*, meaning he delayed him and held him back, as in His words: ﴿they will go around between it and a scalding hot water (*hamim an*)﴾ [al-Rahman: 44]. al-Wahidi said: "The exegetes said: if a single drop from it fell upon the mountains of this world, they would melt."

When He, glorified be He, mentioned their drink, He followed it with the mention of their food, saying: ﴿They will have no food except from *dari'*﴾. It is a kind of thorn called *al-shibriq* in the dialect of Quraysh when it is fresh, and when it dries it becomes *al-dari'*.

Thus said Mujahid, Qatadah, and other exegetes.

It has been said that it is a deadly poison, and when it dries no animal approaches it or grazes on it. It has also been said that it is a thing the sea casts up, called *al-dari'*, one of the food of livestock, not of human beings. If camels graze on it, they do not become satisfied and perish from emaciation.

al-Khalil said: "*Al-dari'* is a green plant with a foul smell that the sea casts up."

The majority of lexicographers and exegetes followed the first view, and from it is the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

(p-1615)
*He grazed on the lush shibriq until, when it withered and became dari', the dry stalks departed from him.*

al-Hudhali, describing camels and the evil of their pasture, said:

*And a detention in the decrepitude of the dari', and all of them are horned, bleeding at the hands, with worn-out hooves.*

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "*Al-dari'* is stones." It has also been said it is a tree in the Fire of Jahannam.

al-Hasan said: "It is among what Allah has hidden of the punishment."

Ibn Kaysan said: "It is a food at which they humble themselves, abase themselves, and beseech Allah to be freed from it. It is named so because its eater beseeches Allah to be spared it, due to its hatefulness and roughness."

al-Nahhas said: "It may be derived from *al-dari'*, meaning the humble one. That is, from drinking it, he is seized with humility and abasement."

al-Hasan also said: "It is *al-zaqqum*." It has also been said it is a valley in Jahannam. It was already mentioned in surah al-Haqqah: ﴿So there is no friend for him here today, nor any food except *ghislin*﴾ [al-Haqqah: 35–36]. *Al-ghislin* is other than *al-dari'*, as already mentioned. The two verses were reconciled by saying the Fire has levels, so some of them have *al-dari'* as food, and some have *al-ghislin* as food.

Then He, glorified be He, described *al-dari'*, saying: ﴿It neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger﴾. That is, *al-dari'* does not fatten its eater, nor does it remove the hunger he has.

The exegetes said: When this verse was revealed, the polytheists said: "Our camels grow fat on *al-dari'*." So it was revealed: ﴿It neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger﴾. They lied in this claim, for camels do not eat *al-dari'* and do not approach it.

It has also been said that its matter was confused for them, so they assumed it was like other beneficial plants.

Then He, glorified be He, began explaining the state of the people of Paradise, after finishing with the state of the people of the Fire, and said: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾. That is, possessing bliss and splendor. These are the faces of the believers, whose faces became radiant because they witnessed the outcome of their affair and what Allah has prepared for them of good that exceeds description. Similar is His words: ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 24].

Then He said: ﴿Pleased with their striving﴾. That is, pleased with their deeds that they did in this world, because they have been given of the reward what pleased them and comforted their eyes. The "faces" here means their owners, as previously mentioned.

﴿In an elevated garden﴾: elevated in place, raised above other places, or elevated in rank, because in it is what souls desire and eyes delight in.

﴿Where they will hear no idle talk﴾. The majority read *la tasma'* with a *fatha* on the second-person *ta'* and *nasb* on *lagiyah*, meaning: you, O addressee, will not hear, or those faces will not hear.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read with a *ya'* with a *damma*, in the passive voice, and *raf'* on *lagiyah*.

Nafi' read with a *ta'* with a *damma*, in the passive voice, and *raf'* on *lagiyah*.

al-Fadl and al-Jahdari read with a *ya'* with a *fatha*, in the active voice, and *nasb* on *lagiyah*. *Al-laghw* is futile speech.

al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: That is, you will not hear in it a word of idle talk.

It has been said that what is meant by this is lying, falsehood, and disbelief. Qatadah said this. Mujahid said: that is, cursing.

al-Farra' said: "You will not hear in it one swearing an oath with a lie."

al-Kalbi said: "You will not hear in Paradise one swearing an oath, whether a righteous oath or a wicked one."

al-Farra' also said: "You will not hear in the speech of the people of Paradise a word that is void, because they speak only with wisdom and praise of Allah, the Exalted, for what He has provided them of everlasting bliss." This is the most preferred of the views, because an indefinite noun in the context of negation is a form of generality, and there is no basis for restricting this to a specific type of idle talk except by a restricting indicator, which does not exist. *Lagiyah* is either an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning a word that is *lagiyah*, or a soul that is *lagiyah*, or a verbal noun, meaning you will not hear *laghwan* (idle talk).

﴿In it is a flowing spring﴾. It has already been mentioned in surah al-Insan that in it are springs, and "spring" here means springs, as in His words: ﴿a soul will know﴾ [al-Takwir: 14]. Its being "flowing" means its waters flow and gush forth with kinds of pleasant drinks.

al-Kalbi said: "I do not know whether it is water or something else."

﴿In it are raised couches﴾: that is, high, elevated in height, or elevated in rank.

﴿And cups set in place﴾. It has already been mentioned that *al-akwab* is the plural of *kub*, which is a cup without a handle. Its being "set in place" means they are placed before them, and they drink from them.

﴿And cushions arranged in rows﴾. *Al-namariq* are cushions.

al-Wahidi said: "By the agreement of all, its singular is *numruqah*, with a *damma* on the *nun*, and al-Farra' added, from the Arabs by report, *nimriqah* with a *kasra*."

al-Kalbi said: "Cushions arranged in rows, some next to others." From this is the poet's saying:

*And indeed we pass the cup among our drinking companions, between us and Abu Qabus, above the cushions.*

Another said:

*Elders and young men, handsome, their faces upon couches arranged in rows and cushions.*

al-Jawhari, in *al-Sihah*, said: "*Al-numruq* and *al-nimriqah* are a small cushion, and likewise *al-nimriqah* with a *kasra* is a dialect, related by Ya'qub."

﴿And carpets spread out﴾. It means rugs. Their singular is *zurbiy* and *zurbiyah*.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' said: "*Al-zarabi* are the thick cushions that have a thin pile. Their singular is *zarbiyah*. *Al-mabthuthah* means spread out," as Qatadah said.

'Ikrimah said: "Some of them are above others."

al-Wahidi said: "It is possible that the meaning is that they are scattered in the gatherings." al-Qutaybi said the same.

al-Farra' said: "The meaning of *mabthuthah* is abundant." The apparent meaning of *al-bath* is dispersal with abundance, and from it: ﴿And He scattered throughout it creatures of every kind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164].

﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they are created?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach. The *fa'* is for coordination with an implied element, as in its counterparts that have passed more than once. The sentence is directed toward establishing the matter of the Resurrection and deriving proof for it, and so is what follows. *Kayfa* is in the accusative, governed by what follows it. The clause is in the genitive position, as a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*) for "the camels." The meaning is: do they deny the matter of the Resurrection and consider its occurrence improbable? Do they not look at the camels, which are the majority of their livestock and the greatest of the created things they see, ﴿how they are created﴾, in the wondrous creation they have, from the immensity of their bodies, their great strength, and their wondrous attributes?

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "He singled out the camels because they are among the quadrupeds that kneel down, so loads are carried upon them, whereas other quadrupeds are not loaded unless they are standing."

al-Zajjaj said: "He alerted them to a great creature of His creation that He has made subservient to the small one: it leads it, makes it kneel, makes it rise, and carries heavy loads upon it while it is kneeling, and it rises with the weight of its load. This is not the case with any other load-bearing animal. Thus He showed them a great part of His creation, so that by it He might prove His oneness."

al-Hasan was asked about this verse, and it was said to him: "The elephant is more wondrous." He said: "As for the elephant, the Arabs are far removed from it in time. Moreover, it is a pig that is not ridden, its meat is not eaten, and its milk is not milked. Whereas the camel is among the most precious and valuable property of the Arabs. It eats date pits and fodder, produces milk, and a child takes hold of its halter and leads it wherever he wishes, despite its greatness in itself."

al-Mubarrad said: "The camels here are the great masses of clouds." This is contrary to what the exegetes and lexicographers mentioned.

It is related from al-Asma'i that he said: "Whoever reads *khuliqat* with the light form means the camel, and whoever reads with the doubled form means the clouds."

﴿And at the sky, how it is raised﴾: that is, raised above the earth without pillars, in a manner that understanding cannot grasp and the intellect cannot comprehend. It has been said: it is raised so nothing can reach it.

﴿And at the mountains, how they are set firm﴾ upon the earth, fixed firmly, not swaying, not leaning, not moving.

﴿And at the earth, how it is spread out﴾: that is, spread flat. *Al-sath* is the spreading of a thing. It is said of the roof of a house when it is level: *sath*.

The majority read *suthihat* in the passive voice with a light form. al-Hasan read with a doubled form. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn al-Sumayfa', and Abu al-'Aliyah read: "*khalaqtu, rafa'tu, nasabtu, sathahtu*" in the active voice, with a *damma* on the *ta'* in all of them.

Then He, glorified be He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to remind, saying: ﴿So remind﴾. The *fa'* is for the sequence of what follows upon what precedes: that is, admonish them, O Muhammad, and warn them. Then He gave the reason for the command to remind, saying: ﴿You are only a reminder﴾. That is, there is nothing upon you except that.

﴿You are not over them a controller﴾. *Al-musaytir* and *al-musayțir* with *sin* and *sad*: one who is empowered over a thing to oversee it and take care of its affairs, as in *al-Sihah*. That is: you are not over them a controller, so as to compel them to faith. This is abrogated (*mansukh*) by the verse of the sword.

The majority read *bi-musaytir* with a *sad*. Hisham and Qunbul, in one narration, read it with a *sin*. Khalaf read it with the *sad* pronounced with a hint of *zay* (*ishmam*). Harun al-A'war read it with a *fatha* on the *ta'*, as a passive participle.

﴿Except for whoever turns away and disbelieves﴾. This is a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*): that is, but whoever turns away from admonition and reminder.

Then God will punish him with the greatest punishment. This is the lasting punishment of Hell. It has also been said that this is a connected exception (al-istithna' al-muttasil, an exception linked to what precedes it) from His saying "so remind," meaning: remind everyone except the one whose hope of his faith has been cut off and who turned away, so he deserves the greatest punishment. The first view is preferable.

It is called "the greatest" because they were already punished in this world by hunger, drought, killing and captivity.

Ibn Mas'ud recited "فإنه يعذبه الله" ("then He punishes him"). Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah recited "ألا من تولى" ("Unquestionably, whoever turns away"), taking "ألا" as the particle of alerting and opening.

Indeed, to Us is their return (iyabahum): that is, their return after death. It is said: "āba yaʾūbu" means he returned. From this is the saying of 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras:

"Every one who has been absent returns,
but the one absent by death does not return."

The majority recited "إيابهم" with light emphasis, while Abu Ja'far and Shaybah recited it with doubled emphasis (تشديد). Abu Hatim said: doubling is not permitted, and if it were, the same would be permitted in "al-siyam" and "al-qiyam." It has also been said that both are dialectal forms with the same meaning.

al-Wahidi said: As for "إيابهم" with a doubled yā', it is anomalous (shadhdh), and no one permitted it except al-Zajjaj.

Then indeed upon Us is their reckoning: meaning their recompense after their return to God through resurrection. "Thumma" (then) here indicates a gap in rank, because the station of reckoning in severity is far above the station of return.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "al-Ghashiyah" is one of the names of the Resurrection.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning "Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming (al-ghashiyah)?" that he said: it is the Hour. "Faces that Day will be humbled, labouring, weary" he said: they will labour and toil in the Fire. "They will be given to drink from a boiling spring" he said: it is the one whose heat has reached its extreme. "They will have no food except from ḍarīʿ" he said: it is shibriq.

Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him: "Faces that Day will be humbled, labouring, weary" he said: this refers to the Jews and the Christians; they humble themselves, but their deeds do not benefit them. "They will be given to drink from a boiling spring" he said: its boiling has reached its peak.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him concerning His saying "They will burn in a Fire of intense heat": he said: it is scorching. "They will be given to drink from a boiling spring": he said: its heat has reached its limit. "They will have no food except from ḍarīʿ": he said: from a tree of fire.

'Abd ibn Humayd also related from him: "except from ḍarīʿ": he said: dry shibriq.

Ibn Jarir also related from him: "You will not hear in it any idle talk": he said: you will not hear harm or falsehood. Concerning His saying "In it are raised couches": he said: some of them above others. "And cushions": he said: gatherings.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him: "And cushions": he said: the armrests (al-marafiq).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him concerning "You are not over them a controller": he said: a tyrant. "Except one who turns away and disbelieves": he said: his reckoning is with God.

Abu Dawud related in his book on abrogation (Nasikh, on naskh, the abrogation of rulings), from him: "You are not over them a controller." Then this was abrogated by His saying: "Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them" [al-Tawbah 9:5]. Ibn al-Mundhir related from him: "Indeed, to Us is their return": he said: their place of return.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 89, verses 1–5 (part 1 of 4):

It is Meccan (Makki) according to the majority of scholars.

Al-Dahhak said: It is Medinan (Madani).

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: The surah ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ was revealed in Mecca.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn al-Zubayr and ʿAʾishah the same.

Al-Bukhari and others related from al-Baraʾ ibn ʿAzib that he said: "The first of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ to come to us was Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr and Ibn Umm Maktum, and they began teaching us the Qur'an. Then ʿAmmar, Bilal and Saʿd came. Then ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab came with twenty men. Then the Prophet ﷺ came, and I did not see the people of Medina rejoice at anything as they rejoiced at him, until I saw the young women and the children saying: This is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ who has come. He had not come until I had recited ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ and the like of it in a surah."

Ahmad, al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh related from ʿAli that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to love this surah: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾."

Ahmad, Muslim and the authors of the Sunan related from al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite in the two ʿEids and on Friday ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ and ﴿Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?﴾. If the two occurred on the same day, he recited both of them." In another wording: "Sometimes both came together on one day, and he recited both of them." There are other hadiths on this topic.

Muslim and others related from Jabir ibn Samurah that "the Prophet ﷺ used to recite ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ in the Zuhr prayer."

Abu Dawud, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi related from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray the Witr with ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾, and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾."

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim (who declared it sound) and al-Bayhaqi related from ʿAʾishah that she said: "The Prophet ﷺ used to recite in the Witr, in the first rakʿah, ﴿Glorify﴾, in the second ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾, and in the third ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ and the two refuges (al-Muʿawwidhatayn)." In the Two Sahihs (al-Sahihayn) it is related that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Muʿadh: Why did you not pray with ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾, and ﴿By the night when it covers﴾?" [i.e., the surah of the Night].

(p-1611)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ means: Exalt Him above everything that is not fitting for Him.

Al-Suddi said: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ means: Magnify Him. It has been said that "name" (al-ism) here is inserted (muqhamah) for the purpose of magnification, as in the verse of Labid:

*"Until the year is complete, and peace be upon you both; whoever weeps for a full year has indeed made an excuse."*

The meaning is: Glorify your Lord, the Most High.

Ibn Jarir said: The meaning is: Exalt the name of your Lord from being named by anyone other than Him. Thus, according to this, it is not inserted.

It has been said that the meaning is: Exalt the naming of your Lord and your mention of Him, that you do not mention Him except while humble and magnifying, and respectful of His remembrance.

Al-Hasan said: The meaning of ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ is: Pray to Him.

It has been said that the meaning is: Pray with the names of Allah, not as the polytheists pray with whistling (al-mukaʾ) and clapping (al-tasdiyah).

It has been said that the meaning is: Raise your voice in the remembrance of your Lord. From this is the saying of Jarir:

*"May Allah disfigure the faces of Taghlib, whenever the pilgrims glorify and proclaim the greatness of God with proclamation."*

"The Most High" (al-aʿla) is an attribute of the Lord, and it has been said that it is an attribute of the name. The first is more preferable.

His saying: ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾ is another attribute of the Lord.

Al-Zajjaj said: He created man upright (mustawiyan), and the meaning of "proportioned" (sawwa) is that He made his stature balanced (ʿadala qamatahu).

Al-Dahhak said: He created him and proportioned his creation. It has been said: He created the bodies and proportioned the faculties of understanding. It has been said: He created man and prepared him for legal responsibility (al-taklif).

﴿And who determined and guided﴾ is another attribute of the Lord, or it is conjoined (maʿtuf) to the relative clause preceding it.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, al-Kisaʾi and al-Sulami read "qadar" (determined) with light stress, and the rest read it with the doubled letter (tashdid). Al-Wahidi said: The commentators said: He determined the creation of the male and the female among the animals, and He guided the male to the female, how he should mount her.

Mujahid said: He guided man to the path of good and evil, and to happiness and misery.

It was also related from him that he said regarding the meaning of the verse: He determined happiness and misery and guided to right guidance and error, and He guided the cattle to their pastures.

It has been said: He determined their provisions and sustenance, and guided them to their livelihoods if they are humans, and to their pastures if they are wild animals.

ʿAtaʾ said: For every creature there was appointed what sustains it, and He guided it to that.

It has been said: He created the benefits in things, and guided man to the way of extracting them from them.

Al-Suddi said: He determined the period of the fetus in the womb as nine months, or less or more, then He guided it to come out of the womb.

Al-Farraʾ said: That is, He determined and guided, and He misguided (aḍalla), so one of the two was mentioned and the other omitted. There are sayings concerning the interpretation of the verse other than what we have mentioned.

The preferable view is not to specify one individual or several individuals of what the words "determined" and "guided" apply to, unless there is evidence indicating it. In the absence of evidence, it is to be understood as applying to whatever the meaning of the two verbs covers, either by substitution (al-badal) or by comprehensiveness (al-shumul). The meaning is: He determined the kinds of things, their types, their attributes, their actions, their sayings and their terms, and He guided each one of them to what proceeds from it and what befits it, and He facilitated for it what it was created for, and He inspired it toward the affairs of its religion and its worldly life.

﴿And who brought forth the pasture﴾ is another attribute of the Lord: that is, He caused the herbage to grow, and the green plants which the cattle graze.

﴿Then made it dark stubble (ghuthaʾan aḥwa)﴾: that is, after it was green, He made it stubble (ghuthaʾ), that is, dry crumbled herbage like the debris that rides atop a flood. "Aḥwa" means black after its greenness, because when the herbage dries it turns black.

Qatadah said: "Ghuthaʾ" is dry matter. It is said of herbs and grass when they are broken and dried: ghuthaʾ and hashim.

Imru' al-Qays said:

*"As if the tops of the head of al-Mujaymir in the morning, from the flood and the debris, were a spindle-whorl."*

The accusative of "ghuthaʾan" is either as the second object, or as a circumstantial state (hal), and "aḥwa" is an attribute of it.

Al-Kisaʾi said: It is a state of "the pasture": that is, He brought it forth black from the intensity of its greenness and irrigation, then after that He made it stubble. "Aḥwa" is derived from "al-ḥuwwah," which is a blackness inclining toward green.

In al-Sihah it is said: "al-ḥuwwah" is the darkness of the lip, and from this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

*"Lamyaʾ (a woman with dark lips), in her lips is ḥuwwah of lʿas, and in her gums and in her canine teeth is shanab."*

﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾: that is, We shall make you a reciter, by inspiring you with recitation, so you will not forget what you recite. The sentence is resumptive (mustaʾnafah), to explain his ﷺ special guidance after the explanation of the general guidance, and it is his ﷺ guidance to memorize the Qur'an.

Mujahid and al-Kalbi said: "When Gabriel came down to the Prophet ﷺ with the revelation, Gabriel did not finish the last part of the verse before the Prophet ﷺ began speaking the first part of it, for fear that he would forget it. So ﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾ was revealed."

His saying: ﴿except what Allah wills﴾ is an exceptive (istithnaʾ mufarragh) from the most general of the objects: that is, you will not forget anything of what you recite except what Allah wills that you forget.

Al-Farraʾ said: He, glorified is He, did not will that Muhammad ﷺ forget anything, like His saying: ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾ [Hud: 107]. It has been said: "except what Allah wills" means that you forget, then you remember after that. So he forgets, but he remembers, and does not forget anything with a complete forgetting.

It has been said that it means naskh (abrogation), that is: except what Allah wills to abrogate its recitation.

It has been said that the meaning of ﴿so you will not forget﴾ is: so do not abandon acting upon it, except what Allah wills that you abandon, because of its abrogation and the lifting of its ruling.

It has been said that the meaning is: except what Allah wills to delay its sending down.

It has been said that the "lā" in His saying ﴿so you will not forget﴾ is a prohibition (lā al-nahy). The alif is added for the sake of the rhyme (fawasil), as in His saying: ﴿So they misled us from the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67]. The meaning is: do not neglect its recitation, and remember it.

﴿Indeed He knows the open and what is hidden﴾: this sentence is a justification (taʿlil) for what precedes it: that is, He knows what is manifest and what is concealed, and the public and the private. Its apparent meaning is generality, so there falls under it what has been said: that the "open" is what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ memorized of the Qur'an, and what is "hidden" is what was abrogated from his heart. Also falling under it is what has been said: that the open is the public declaration of charity, and what is hidden is concealing it. Also falling under it is what has been said: that the open is his ﷺ recitation of the Qur'an aloud along with Gabriel's recitation, for fear that it would slip from him, and what is hidden is what is in his soul of what calls him to speak aloud.

﴿And We shall ease you toward ease﴾ is conjoined to "We shall make you recite," and what is between them is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtiraḍ).

Muqatil said: That is, We shall make easy for you the work of Paradise. It has been said: We shall grant you success in the way that is easier and simpler. It has been said: toward the easy law, which is the straightforward, easy monotheism (al-hanifiyyah al-samhah). It has been said: We shall make easy for you the revelation until you memorize it and act upon it. (p-1612) The preferable view is to take the verse in its generality: that is, We shall grant you success in the easiest way in religion and in worldly life, in every matter of theirs that comes to you.

﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾: that is, admonish, O Muhammad, the people with what We have revealed to you, guide them to the paths of good, and direct them to the laws of religion.

Al-Hasan said: It is a reminder for the believer and a proof against the disbeliever.

Al-Wahidi said: "If it benefits or does not benefit." He did not mention the second case, like His saying: ﴿Garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], the verse.

Al-Jurjani said: Reminding is obligatory even if it does not benefit; so the meaning is: whether the reminder benefits or does not benefit.

It has been said that it is specific to a particular people by their persons. It has been said: "in" (in) here means "mā" (what): that is, remind with what the reminder benefited, because the reminder is beneficial in every case. It has been said that it means "qad" (indeed). It has been said that it means "idh" (when).

What al-Wahidi and al-Jurjani said is preferable, and al-Farraʾ and al-Nahhas preceded them to saying it.

Al-Razi said: His saying "if the reminder benefits" is to draw attention to the more noble of the two states, which is the existence of the benefit for the sake of which the reminder was prescribed. What is conditioned by "in" on a thing does not necessarily imply that it is nonexistent when that thing is absent. Several verses prove this: among them this verse; among them His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And be grateful to Allah, if you are indeed worshipping Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172]; among them His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer if you fear﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 101], for shortening is permissible both in fear and in its absence; among them His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon them both for returning to each other if they think they can keep the limits of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230], and returning is permissible without this supposition. So this condition has benefits: among them what has preceded, and among them the stimulation toward benefiting from the reminder, as a man says to one he is guiding: "I have clarified it for you, if you understand," and it is an admonition to the Prophet ﷺ that they will not benefit from the reminder. Or this may be in the repetition of the call, whereas the first call is general. End of quotation.

Then He, glorified is He, explained the difference between the one whom the reminder benefits and the one whom it does not benefit, and said: ﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾, that is, whoever fears Allah will be admonished by your admonition, and his fear and righteousness will increase through the reminder.

﴿But the most wretched will avoid it﴾: that is, the most wretched of the disbelievers will avoid and keep far from the reminder, because of his persistence in disbelief in Allah and his immersion in His disobedience.

Then He described the most wretched, saying: ﴿Who will enter the greatest Fire﴾, that is, the magnificent and dreadful one, because it is more intense in heat than others.

Al-Hasan said: "The greatest Fire" is the Fire of Hell, and "the lesser Fire" is the Fire of this world.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is the lowest of the layers of the Fire.

﴿Then he will neither die therein nor live﴾: that is, he will not die therein so as to find rest from the punishment he is in, nor will he live a life from which he benefits. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Ah, what is with a soul that does not die so that its distress ends, nor lives a life that has any sweetness?"*

"Then" (thumma) here indicates delay in degrees of severity, because oscillation between death and life is more dreadful than burning in the greatest Fire.

﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies himself﴾: that is, who purified himself from polytheism, so he believed in Allah, declared His oneness, and acted in accordance with His laws.

ʿAtaʾ and al-Rabiʿ said: whoever's deed is pure and growing.

Qatadah said: "He purified himself by righteous deed."

Qatadah, ʿAtaʾ and Abu al-ʿAliyah said: It was revealed concerning the charity of breaking the fast (ṣadaqat al-fitr).

ʿIkrimah said: A man would say: "I give my zakat before my prayer."

The root of zakat in language is growth (al-namaʾ).

It has been said that the intended meaning of the verse is the zakat of all wealth.

It has been said that the intended meaning is the purification of deeds, not the zakat of wealth, because most often one says of wealth "zakka" (he purified), not "tazakka" (he purified himself).

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 87, verses 14–15, and surah 88, verses 1–7**

﴿And he remembers the name of his Lord and prays.﴾ It has been said that the meaning is: he remembers the name of his Lord in fear, so he worships Him and prays to Him. It has also been said: he remembers the name of his Lord with his tongue and prays, that is, he establishes the five prayers.

It has been said: he remembers his standing before Him and his return to Him, so he worships Him, and this is similar to the first view.

It has been said: he remembers the name of his Lord by saying the takbir (the saying "Allahu akbar") at the beginning of the prayer, because the prayer is not validly begun except with that remembrance. It has been said: he remembers the name of his Lord on the way to the prayer-place and then prays. It has been said: it means that he performs a voluntary prayer after giving zakāt. It has been said: the prayer here means the festival prayer (ṣalāt al-ʿīd), just as the purification in the first verse means zakāt al-fiṭr (the obligatory charity paid at the end of Ramadan). But this view is far-fetched, because the sūrah is Meccan, and zakāt al-fiṭr and the festival prayer were not made obligatory except in Madina.

﴿Rather, you prefer the worldly life.﴾ This is a turning away (iḍrāb) from an implied statement that the context indicates: that is, "You do not do that; rather, you prefer the fleeting pleasures of this world."

Most readers recite *tu’thirūna* with a *fawqiyyah* (the letter ta at the top, i.e., second person, "you prefer"), addressing the audience directly. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: *bal antum tu’thirūna* ("rather, you yourselves prefer"). Abu ʿAmr read it with a *taḥtiyyah* (the letter ya at the bottom, i.e., third person, "they prefer").

It has been said that the verse refers to the disbelievers, and that preferring the worldly life means being content with it, being at ease with it, and turning away completely from the Hereafter. It has also been said that it refers to all people, believers and disbelievers alike, and that "preferring" here means something more general: what is not free of most people, namely that the worldly side outweighs the Hereafter, and that they turn toward gaining its benefits and give it greater concern than they give to acts of obedience.

﴿And the Hereafter is better and more lasting.﴾ This is in a position of accusative (naṣb) as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of *tu’thirūna*: that is, "while the Hereafter, which is Paradise, is better and more enduring than this world." Mālik ibn Dīnār said: "If the world were made of gold that perishes, and the Hereafter were made of pottery that endures, it would be obligatory to prefer the enduring pottery over the perishing gold. How much more so when the Hereafter is of gold that endures and the world is of pottery that perishes?"

﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures.﴾ The demonstrative *hādhā* ("this") refers to what preceded: the success of the one who purifies himself and what follows it. It has also been said that it refers to the whole sūrah. The meaning of *fī al-ṣuḥuf al-ūlā* ("in the former scrolls") is that it is established in them.

﴿The scrolls of Abraham and Moses.﴾ This is a substitute (badal) for "the former scrolls."

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: by his saying "indeed, this" is meant that the Hereafter is better and more lasting. And they both said: the books of Allah, mighty and majestic, agreed that the Hereafter is better and more lasting than this world.

Al-Ḥasan said: the books of Allah, may His praise be exalted, agreed that "indeed, this is in the former scrolls," which is His saying "He has succeeded" up to the end of the sūrah.

Most readers recite *ṣuḥufi* with a *ḍammah* on the *ḥāʾ* in both places. Al-Aʿmash, Hārūn, and Abu ʿAmr in one narration read it with a *sukūn* (no vowel) on it in both places. Most readers recite *Ibrāhīm* with an *alif* after the *rāʾ* and a *yāʾ* after the *hāʾ*. Abu Rajāʾ read it without these two letters and with a *fatḥah* on the *hāʾ*. Abu Mūsā and Ibn al-Zubayr read *Ibrāhām* with two *alifs*.

Aḥmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿUqba ibn ʿĀmir al-Juhani, who said: "When *fasabbiḥ bi-smi rabbika al-ʿaẓīm* (So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty) [al-Ḥāqqa: 52] was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to us: 'Place it in your bowing (rukūʿ).' When *sabbiḥ ismа rabbika al-aʿlā* (Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High) was revealed [that is, the sūrah al-Aʿlā], he said: 'Place it in your prostration (sujūd).'" There is no objection to its chain of narration.

Aḥmad, Abu Dawud, al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that "when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited *sabbiḥ ismа rabbika al-aʿlā*, he would say: *subḥāna rabbiya al-aʿlā* (Glory be to my Lord, the Most High)."

Abu Dawud said: Waki' disagreed with this, for Shuʿba narrated it from Abu Ishaq, from Saʿid, from Ibn ʿAbbas, as a statement of his own (mawqūf).

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, and Ibn Jarir also narrated it as a statement of Ibn ʿAbbas (mawqūf): that when he recited *sabbiḥ ismа rabbika al-aʿlā* he would say: *subḥāna rabbiya al-aʿlā*. In a wording of ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd from him: "When you recite *sabbiḥ ismа rabbika al-aʿlā*, say: *subḥāna rabbiya al-aʿlā*."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, and Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Maṣāḥif* narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Ṭalib that he recited *sabbiḥ ismа rabbika al-aʿlā* and said: *subḥāna rabbiya al-aʿlā*, while he was in the prayer. He was asked: "Are you adding to the Qur'an?" He said: "No, but he commanded us with something, so I said it."

Al-Firyabi, Saʿid ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu Mūsā al-Ashʿari that he recited *sabbiḥ ismа rabbika al-aʿlā* in the Friday prayer, and said: *subḥāna rabbiya al-aʿlā*.

Saʿid ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr who said: "I heard Ibn ʿUmar reciting *sabbiḥ ismа rabbika al-aʿlā*, and he said: *subḥāna rabbiya al-aʿlā*." And it is like this in the reading of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.

Ibn Abi Shayba and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that he recited *sabbiḥ ismа rabbika al-aʿlā* and said: *subḥāna rabbiya al-aʿlā*, while he was in the prayer.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying *fajaʿalahu ghuthāʾan* (and made it debris): "*Hashīman*" (dry stubble), *aḥwā* ("dark"), he said: "changed."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to rehearse the Qur'an out of fear of forgetting it, so it was said to him: 'We have spared you that,' and *sanuqri'uka fa-lā tansā* (We will make you recite, so you will not forget) was revealed."

al-Ḥākim narrated similarly from Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas.

Ibn Abi Ḥatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding *illā mā shāʾa Allāh* (except what Allah wills): he would say, "*illā mā shiʾta anā fa-unsīka*" (except what I will, then I make you forget).

Ibn Abi Ḥatim also narrated from him: *wa-nuyassiruka lil-yusrā* (and We will ease you toward ease) he said: "toward good."

Ibn Abi Ḥatim narrated from Ibn Masʿud: *wa-nuyassiruka lil-yusrā*, he said: "Paradise."

al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying *qad aflaḥa man tazakkā* (He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself), that he said: "It is whoever bears witness that there is no god but Allah, renounces rivals (andād), and bears witness that I am the Messenger of Allah." And *wa-dhakara isma rabbihi fa-ṣallā* (and remembers the name of his Lord and prays): "These are the five prayers, and guarding them and being concerned with their proper times."

Al-Bazzar said: "This is not narrated from Jabir except through this route."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Ḥatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying *qad aflaḥa man tazakkā*: "from polytheism." *Wa-dhakara isma rabbihi*: "he affirmed the oneness of Allah," *fa-ṣallā*: "the five prayers."

al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asmāʾ wa-l-Ṣifāt* narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding *qad aflaḥa man tazakkā*: "he who says *lā ilāha illā Allāh*."

al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim, al-Ḥākim in *al-Kunā*, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Kathir ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that "he used to command zakāt al-fiṭr before performing the festival prayer, and he would recite this verse: *qad aflaḥa man tazakkā wa-dhakara isma rabbihi fa-ṣallā*."

In another wording: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about zakāt al-fiṭr, and he said: *qad aflaḥa man tazakkā*, and said: 'It is zakāt al-fiṭr.'" But Kathir ibn ʿAbd Allah is extremely weak. Abu Dawud said of him: "He is one of the pillars of falsehood." Al-Tirmidhi authenticated a hadith through his route, but this was judged to be an error. However, what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri supports it, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: *qad aflaḥa man tazakkā wa-dhakara isma rabbihi fa-ṣallā*, then he would distribute the charity (fiṭra) before going out to the prayer-place on the day of al-Fiṭr." There is nothing in these two hadiths that indicates that this was the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl); rather, in them he (ﷺ) only recited the verse. As for his saying "it is zakāt al-fiṭr," it may mean that it is among the things to which the word *tazakkī* (purification) applies. We have already mentioned that the sūrah is Meccan, and there was no festival prayer or fiṭra charity in Mecca.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri regarding *qad aflaḥa man tazakkā*: "he gave the charity of fiṭr before he went out to the festival," and *wa-dhakara isma rabbihi fa-ṣallā*: "he went out to the festival and prayed."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "This verse was only revealed about the giving of the fiṭr charity before the festival prayer: *qad aflaḥa man tazakkā* and *wa-dhakara isma rabbihi fa-ṣallā*."

Ibn Abi Ḥatim narrated from ʿAṭāʾ who said: "I said to Ibn ʿAbbas: 'What do you think of His saying *qad aflaḥa man tazakkā*? Is it about fiṭr?' He said: 'I have not heard of that, but it is about all zakāt.' Then I asked him again, and he said to me: 'And all charities.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ṭabarānī, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shuʿab al-Īmān* narrated from ʿArfaja al-Thaqafi who said: "I asked Ibn Masʿud to recite *sabbiḥ ismа rabbika al-aʿlā* for me, and when he reached *bal tu'thirūna al-ḥayāt al-dunyā* (rather, you prefer the worldly life), he stopped reciting, turned to his companions, and said: 'We preferred the world over the Hereafter.' The people were silent, and he said: 'We preferred the world because we saw its adornment, its women, its food, and its drink, while the Hereafter was hidden from us. So we chose this immediate thing and left the deferred one.'" And he recited *bal yu'thirūna al-ḥayāt al-dunyā* with the *yāʾ* (third person).

al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding "*inna hādhā lafī al-ṣuḥuf al-ūlā ṣuḥufi Ibrāhīm wa-Mūsā*" (indeed, this is in the former scrolls, the scrolls of Abraham and Moses), he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'It is all in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses.'"

Saʿid ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning the verse: "This sūrah was abrogated (nusikhat) from the scrolls of Abraham and Moses." In another wording: "This sūrah is in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Abu Dharr, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how many books did Allah send down?' He said: 'One hundred books and four books.'" The hadith continues.

* *

Ibn al-Ḍurays, al-Naḥḥās, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "The sūrah al-Ghāshiya was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr. And the hadith of al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr has already passed: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite *sabbiḥ ismа rabbika al-aʿlā* and al-Ghāshiya in the festival prayer and on Friday."

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

His saying: *hal atāka ḥadīth al-ghāshiya* (Has there come to you the news of the Overwhelming?) Several exegetes said: "*Hal*" here means *qad* (indeed), and Quṭrub said likewise: that is, "The news of the Overwhelming has indeed come to you, O Muḥammad." The Overwhelming is the Resurrection, because it overwhelms creatures with its terrors.

It has also been said that keeping *hal* here in its interrogative meaning, which implies amazement at its report and arousing eagerness to hear it, is better.

Most exegetes went to the view that the Overwhelming here means the Resurrection.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb said: "The Overwhelming is the Fire, which covers the faces of the disbelievers, as in His saying: *wa-taghshā wujūhahumu al-nār* (and the Fire will cover their faces) [Ibrāhīm: 50]." It has also been said that the Overwhelming is the people of the Fire, because they overwhelm it and plunge into it. The first view is better.

al-Kalbi said: "The meaning is: if the news of the Overwhelming has not come to you, then it has come to you now."

*Wujūhun yawma'idhin khāshiʿa* (Faces that day will be humbled). This sentence is a new statement (mustaʾnafa), an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What is it?" Or it is a grammatical new sentence to explain what the phrase contains of a state of affairs. Then "faces" on that day are described by this described attribute. *Wujūh* is in the nominative case as a subject, even though it is indefinite, because it occurs in a context of detailed explanation. A similar thing has already passed in the sūrah al-Qiyāma and in the sūrah al-Nāziʿāt.

The nunation in *yawma'idhin* (that day) is a replacement for the omitted genitive: that is, "the day of the coming of the Overwhelming." *Khāshiʿa* means humbled, abased. Anything that is subdued and still is called *khāshiʿ*. It is said: "the sound was humbled" when it became faint, and "he was humbled in his prayer" when he became submissive and lowered his head.

The word "faces" here refers to their owners.

Muqatil said: "It means the disbelievers, because they were arrogant toward worshipping Allah."

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: "Humbled in the Fire." It has also been said that it means the faces of the Jews and Christians specifically.

The first view is better.

His saying: *ʿāmila nāṣiba* (laboring, toiling). The meaning of *ʿāmila* is that they do laborious work.

The lexicographers said: "It is said of a man when he persists in his journey: '*ʿamila yaʿmalu ʿamalan*' (he labored, labors, labor), and it is said of a cloud when its lightning persists: 'it has labored, labors, labor.'"

Al-Shawkani's Fath al-Qadir, on surah 89, verses 1–5 (part 3 of 4):

It has been said that this work is dragging chains and shackles and wading through the Fire. *Nasibah* means weary (*ta'biyah*). It is said that *nasiba* (with the vowel *kasra*) *yansabu nasaban* means to become weary. The meaning is that in the Hereafter they will be weary because of what they encounter of the punishment of Allah.

It has also been said that His words "working, toiling" refer to this world, since there is no work in the Hereafter. That is, they work in this world in disbelief and sins, and they toil in that.

It has also been said that they work in this world and toil in the Hereafter. The first view is preferable.

Qatadah said: "﴿Working, toiling﴾: they were arrogant in this world toward obedience to Allah, so Allah made them work and made them toil in the Fire, by dragging heavy chains, carrying shackles, and standing barefoot and naked in the open plains, ﴿on a day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4]."

al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "They did not work for Allah in this world and did not toil, so Allah makes them work and toil in Jahannam."

al-Kalbi said: "They are dragged on their faces in the Fire."

He also said: "They are obliged to climb a mountain of iron in Jahannam, and they toil there at the utmost degree of toil, by handling chains and shackles and wading through the Fire, as camels wade through mud."

The majority of readers (qira'at) read ﴿working, toiling﴾ with *raf'* (nominative) in both words, as two further predicates of the subject, or with an implied subject of which these two are predicates. Ibn Muhaysin, 'Isa, Humayd, and Ibn Kathir in one narration from him read both with *nasb* (accusative), as circumstantial accusatives (*hal*) or as accusatives of dispraise (*dhamm*).

His words ﴿they will burn in a blazing Fire﴾ are another predicate of the subject. That is, they will enter a fire extremely intense in heat. It is said: "The day became hot" (*hamiya al-nahar*) and "the oven became hot" (*hamiya al-tannur*), meaning its heat intensified.

al-Kisa'i said: "It is said *ishtadda hamy al-nahar* and *hamwuhu* with the same meaning."

The majority read *tasla* with a *fatha* on the *ta'*, in the active voice. Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, and Abu Bakr read both with a *damma*, in the passive voice. Abu Ra'ja' read with a *damma* on the *ta'*, a *fatha* on the *sad*, and a shadda on the *lam*. The pronoun refers to the faces (*wujuh*) in all these readings, and what is meant is their owners, as previously mentioned. The pronoun is the same.

﴿They will be given drink from a boiling spring﴾. The "boiling spring" (*'ayn aniyah*) means one extremely hot. *Aniy* is that which has reached the end of its heat, from *al-iyna'*, meaning delay. It is said *anahu yu'nihi in'a'an*, meaning he delayed him and held him back, as in His words: ﴿they will go around between it and a scalding hot water (*hamim an*)﴾ [al-Rahman: 44]. al-Wahidi said: "The exegetes said: if a single drop from it fell upon the mountains of this world, they would melt."

When He, glorified be He, mentioned their drink, He followed it with the mention of their food, saying: ﴿They will have no food except from *dari'*﴾. It is a kind of thorn called *al-shibriq* in the dialect of Quraysh when it is fresh, and when it dries it becomes *al-dari'*.

Thus said Mujahid, Qatadah, and other exegetes.

It has been said that it is a deadly poison, and when it dries no animal approaches it or grazes on it. It has also been said that it is a thing the sea casts up, called *al-dari'*, one of the food of livestock, not of human beings. If camels graze on it, they do not become satisfied and perish from emaciation.

al-Khalil said: "*Al-dari'* is a green plant with a foul smell that the sea casts up."

The majority of lexicographers and exegetes followed the first view, and from it is the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

(p-1615)
*He grazed on the lush shibriq until, when it withered and became dari', the dry stalks departed from him.*

al-Hudhali, describing camels and the evil of their pasture, said:

*And a detention in the decrepitude of the dari', and all of them are horned, bleeding at the hands, with worn-out hooves.*

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "*Al-dari'* is stones." It has also been said it is a tree in the Fire of Jahannam.

al-Hasan said: "It is among what Allah has hidden of the punishment."

Ibn Kaysan said: "It is a food at which they humble themselves, abase themselves, and beseech Allah to be freed from it. It is named so because its eater beseeches Allah to be spared it, due to its hatefulness and roughness."

al-Nahhas said: "It may be derived from *al-dari'*, meaning the humble one. That is, from drinking it, he is seized with humility and abasement."

al-Hasan also said: "It is *al-zaqqum*." It has also been said it is a valley in Jahannam. It was already mentioned in surah al-Haqqah: ﴿So there is no friend for him here today, nor any food except *ghislin*﴾ [al-Haqqah: 35–36]. *Al-ghislin* is other than *al-dari'*, as already mentioned. The two verses were reconciled by saying the Fire has levels, so some of them have *al-dari'* as food, and some have *al-ghislin* as food.

Then He, glorified be He, described *al-dari'*, saying: ﴿It neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger﴾. That is, *al-dari'* does not fatten its eater, nor does it remove the hunger he has.

The exegetes said: When this verse was revealed, the polytheists said: "Our camels grow fat on *al-dari'*." So it was revealed: ﴿It neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger﴾. They lied in this claim, for camels do not eat *al-dari'* and do not approach it.

It has also been said that its matter was confused for them, so they assumed it was like other beneficial plants.

Then He, glorified be He, began explaining the state of the people of Paradise, after finishing with the state of the people of the Fire, and said: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾. That is, possessing bliss and splendor. These are the faces of the believers, whose faces became radiant because they witnessed the outcome of their affair and what Allah has prepared for them of good that exceeds description. Similar is His words: ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 24].

Then He said: ﴿Pleased with their striving﴾. That is, pleased with their deeds that they did in this world, because they have been given of the reward what pleased them and comforted their eyes. The "faces" here means their owners, as previously mentioned.

﴿In an elevated garden﴾: elevated in place, raised above other places, or elevated in rank, because in it is what souls desire and eyes delight in.

﴿Where they will hear no idle talk﴾. The majority read *la tasma'* with a *fatha* on the second-person *ta'* and *nasb* on *lagiyah*, meaning: you, O addressee, will not hear, or those faces will not hear.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read with a *ya'* with a *damma*, in the passive voice, and *raf'* on *lagiyah*.

Nafi' read with a *ta'* with a *damma*, in the passive voice, and *raf'* on *lagiyah*.

al-Fadl and al-Jahdari read with a *ya'* with a *fatha*, in the active voice, and *nasb* on *lagiyah*. *Al-laghw* is futile speech.

al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: That is, you will not hear in it a word of idle talk.

It has been said that what is meant by this is lying, falsehood, and disbelief. Qatadah said this. Mujahid said: that is, cursing.

al-Farra' said: "You will not hear in it one swearing an oath with a lie."

al-Kalbi said: "You will not hear in Paradise one swearing an oath, whether a righteous oath or a wicked one."

al-Farra' also said: "You will not hear in the speech of the people of Paradise a word that is void, because they speak only with wisdom and praise of Allah, the Exalted, for what He has provided them of everlasting bliss." This is the most preferred of the views, because an indefinite noun in the context of negation is a form of generality, and there is no basis for restricting this to a specific type of idle talk except by a restricting indicator, which does not exist. *Lagiyah* is either an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning a word that is *lagiyah*, or a soul that is *lagiyah*, or a verbal noun, meaning you will not hear *laghwan* (idle talk).

﴿In it is a flowing spring﴾. It has already been mentioned in surah al-Insan that in it are springs, and "spring" here means springs, as in His words: ﴿a soul will know﴾ [al-Takwir: 14]. Its being "flowing" means its waters flow and gush forth with kinds of pleasant drinks.

al-Kalbi said: "I do not know whether it is water or something else."

﴿In it are raised couches﴾: that is, high, elevated in height, or elevated in rank.

﴿And cups set in place﴾. It has already been mentioned that *al-akwab* is the plural of *kub*, which is a cup without a handle. Its being "set in place" means they are placed before them, and they drink from them.

﴿And cushions arranged in rows﴾. *Al-namariq* are cushions.

al-Wahidi said: "By the agreement of all, its singular is *numruqah*, with a *damma* on the *nun*, and al-Farra' added, from the Arabs by report, *nimriqah* with a *kasra*."

al-Kalbi said: "Cushions arranged in rows, some next to others." From this is the poet's saying:

*And indeed we pass the cup among our drinking companions, between us and Abu Qabus, above the cushions.*

Another said:

*Elders and young men, handsome, their faces upon couches arranged in rows and cushions.*

al-Jawhari, in *al-Sihah*, said: "*Al-numruq* and *al-nimriqah* are a small cushion, and likewise *al-nimriqah* with a *kasra* is a dialect, related by Ya'qub."

﴿And carpets spread out﴾. It means rugs. Their singular is *zurbiy* and *zurbiyah*.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' said: "*Al-zarabi* are the thick cushions that have a thin pile. Their singular is *zarbiyah*. *Al-mabthuthah* means spread out," as Qatadah said.

'Ikrimah said: "Some of them are above others."

al-Wahidi said: "It is possible that the meaning is that they are scattered in the gatherings." al-Qutaybi said the same.

al-Farra' said: "The meaning of *mabthuthah* is abundant." The apparent meaning of *al-bath* is dispersal with abundance, and from it: ﴿And He scattered throughout it creatures of every kind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164].

﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they are created?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach. The *fa'* is for coordination with an implied element, as in its counterparts that have passed more than once. The sentence is directed toward establishing the matter of the Resurrection and deriving proof for it, and so is what follows. *Kayfa* is in the accusative, governed by what follows it. The clause is in the genitive position, as a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*) for "the camels." The meaning is: do they deny the matter of the Resurrection and consider its occurrence improbable? Do they not look at the camels, which are the majority of their livestock and the greatest of the created things they see, ﴿how they are created﴾, in the wondrous creation they have, from the immensity of their bodies, their great strength, and their wondrous attributes?

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "He singled out the camels because they are among the quadrupeds that kneel down, so loads are carried upon them, whereas other quadrupeds are not loaded unless they are standing."

al-Zajjaj said: "He alerted them to a great creature of His creation that He has made subservient to the small one: it leads it, makes it kneel, makes it rise, and carries heavy loads upon it while it is kneeling, and it rises with the weight of its load. This is not the case with any other load-bearing animal. Thus He showed them a great part of His creation, so that by it He might prove His oneness."

al-Hasan was asked about this verse, and it was said to him: "The elephant is more wondrous." He said: "As for the elephant, the Arabs are far removed from it in time. Moreover, it is a pig that is not ridden, its meat is not eaten, and its milk is not milked. Whereas the camel is among the most precious and valuable property of the Arabs. It eats date pits and fodder, produces milk, and a child takes hold of its halter and leads it wherever he wishes, despite its greatness in itself."

al-Mubarrad said: "The camels here are the great masses of clouds." This is contrary to what the exegetes and lexicographers mentioned.

It is related from al-Asma'i that he said: "Whoever reads *khuliqat* with the light form means the camel, and whoever reads with the doubled form means the clouds."

﴿And at the sky, how it is raised﴾: that is, raised above the earth without pillars, in a manner that understanding cannot grasp and the intellect cannot comprehend. It has been said: it is raised so nothing can reach it.

﴿And at the mountains, how they are set firm﴾ upon the earth, fixed firmly, not swaying, not leaning, not moving.

﴿And at the earth, how it is spread out﴾: that is, spread flat. *Al-sath* is the spreading of a thing. It is said of the roof of a house when it is level: *sath*.

The majority read *suthihat* in the passive voice with a light form. al-Hasan read with a doubled form. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn al-Sumayfa', and Abu al-'Aliyah read: "*khalaqtu, rafa'tu, nasabtu, sathahtu*" in the active voice, with a *damma* on the *ta'* in all of them.

Then He, glorified be He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to remind, saying: ﴿So remind﴾. The *fa'* is for the sequence of what follows upon what precedes: that is, admonish them, O Muhammad, and warn them. Then He gave the reason for the command to remind, saying: ﴿You are only a reminder﴾. That is, there is nothing upon you except that.

﴿You are not over them a controller﴾. *Al-musaytir* and *al-musayțir* with *sin* and *sad*: one who is empowered over a thing to oversee it and take care of its affairs, as in *al-Sihah*. That is: you are not over them a controller, so as to compel them to faith. This is abrogated (*mansukh*) by the verse of the sword.

The majority read *bi-musaytir* with a *sad*. Hisham and Qunbul, in one narration, read it with a *sin*. Khalaf read it with the *sad* pronounced with a hint of *zay* (*ishmam*). Harun al-A'war read it with a *fatha* on the *ta'*, as a passive participle.

﴿Except for whoever turns away and disbelieves﴾. This is a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*): that is, but whoever turns away from admonition and reminder.

Then God will punish him with the greatest punishment. This is the lasting punishment of Hell. It has also been said that this is a connected exception (al-istithna' al-muttasil, an exception linked to what precedes it) from His saying "so remind," meaning: remind everyone except the one whose hope of his faith has been cut off and who turned away, so he deserves the greatest punishment. The first view is preferable.

It is called "the greatest" because they were already punished in this world by hunger, drought, killing and captivity.

Ibn Mas'ud recited "فإنه يعذبه الله" ("then He punishes him"). Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah recited "ألا من تولى" ("Unquestionably, whoever turns away"), taking "ألا" as the particle of alerting and opening.

Indeed, to Us is their return (iyabahum): that is, their return after death. It is said: "āba yaʾūbu" means he returned. From this is the saying of 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras:

"Every one who has been absent returns,
but the one absent by death does not return."

The majority recited "إيابهم" with light emphasis, while Abu Ja'far and Shaybah recited it with doubled emphasis (تشديد). Abu Hatim said: doubling is not permitted, and if it were, the same would be permitted in "al-siyam" and "al-qiyam." It has also been said that both are dialectal forms with the same meaning.

al-Wahidi said: As for "إيابهم" with a doubled yā', it is anomalous (shadhdh), and no one permitted it except al-Zajjaj.

Then indeed upon Us is their reckoning: meaning their recompense after their return to God through resurrection. "Thumma" (then) here indicates a gap in rank, because the station of reckoning in severity is far above the station of return.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "al-Ghashiyah" is one of the names of the Resurrection.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning "Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming (al-ghashiyah)?" that he said: it is the Hour. "Faces that Day will be humbled, labouring, weary" he said: they will labour and toil in the Fire. "They will be given to drink from a boiling spring" he said: it is the one whose heat has reached its extreme. "They will have no food except from ḍarīʿ" he said: it is shibriq.

Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him: "Faces that Day will be humbled, labouring, weary" he said: this refers to the Jews and the Christians; they humble themselves, but their deeds do not benefit them. "They will be given to drink from a boiling spring" he said: its boiling has reached its peak.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him concerning His saying "They will burn in a Fire of intense heat": he said: it is scorching. "They will be given to drink from a boiling spring": he said: its heat has reached its limit. "They will have no food except from ḍarīʿ": he said: from a tree of fire.

'Abd ibn Humayd also related from him: "except from ḍarīʿ": he said: dry shibriq.

Ibn Jarir also related from him: "You will not hear in it any idle talk": he said: you will not hear harm or falsehood. Concerning His saying "In it are raised couches": he said: some of them above others. "And cushions": he said: gatherings.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him: "And cushions": he said: the armrests (al-marafiq).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him concerning "You are not over them a controller": he said: a tyrant. "Except one who turns away and disbelieves": he said: his reckoning is with God.

Abu Dawud related in his book on abrogation (Nasikh, on naskh, the abrogation of rulings), from him: "You are not over them a controller." Then this was abrogated by His saying: "Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them" [al-Tawbah 9:5]. Ibn al-Mundhir related from him: "Indeed, to Us is their return": he said: their place of return.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 89, verses 1–5 (part 1 of 4):

It is Meccan (Makki) according to the majority of scholars.

Al-Dahhak said: It is Medinan (Madani).

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: The surah ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ was revealed in Mecca.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn al-Zubayr and ʿAʾishah the same.

Al-Bukhari and others related from al-Baraʾ ibn ʿAzib that he said: "The first of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ to come to us was Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr and Ibn Umm Maktum, and they began teaching us the Qur'an. Then ʿAmmar, Bilal and Saʿd came. Then ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab came with twenty men. Then the Prophet ﷺ came, and I did not see the people of Medina rejoice at anything as they rejoiced at him, until I saw the young women and the children saying: This is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ who has come. He had not come until I had recited ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ and the like of it in a surah."

Ahmad, al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh related from ʿAli that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to love this surah: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾."

Ahmad, Muslim and the authors of the Sunan related from al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite in the two ʿEids and on Friday ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ and ﴿Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?﴾. If the two occurred on the same day, he recited both of them." In another wording: "Sometimes both came together on one day, and he recited both of them." There are other hadiths on this topic.

Muslim and others related from Jabir ibn Samurah that "the Prophet ﷺ used to recite ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ in the Zuhr prayer."

Abu Dawud, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi related from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray the Witr with ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾, and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾."

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim (who declared it sound) and al-Bayhaqi related from ʿAʾishah that she said: "The Prophet ﷺ used to recite in the Witr, in the first rakʿah, ﴿Glorify﴾, in the second ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾, and in the third ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ and the two refuges (al-Muʿawwidhatayn)." In the Two Sahihs (al-Sahihayn) it is related that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Muʿadh: Why did you not pray with ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾, and ﴿By the night when it covers﴾?" [i.e., the surah of the Night].

(p-1611)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ means: Exalt Him above everything that is not fitting for Him.

Al-Suddi said: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ means: Magnify Him. It has been said that "name" (al-ism) here is inserted (muqhamah) for the purpose of magnification, as in the verse of Labid:

*"Until the year is complete, and peace be upon you both; whoever weeps for a full year has indeed made an excuse."*

The meaning is: Glorify your Lord, the Most High.

Ibn Jarir said: The meaning is: Exalt the name of your Lord from being named by anyone other than Him. Thus, according to this, it is not inserted.

It has been said that the meaning is: Exalt the naming of your Lord and your mention of Him, that you do not mention Him except while humble and magnifying, and respectful of His remembrance.

Al-Hasan said: The meaning of ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ is: Pray to Him.

It has been said that the meaning is: Pray with the names of Allah, not as the polytheists pray with whistling (al-mukaʾ) and clapping (al-tasdiyah).

It has been said that the meaning is: Raise your voice in the remembrance of your Lord. From this is the saying of Jarir:

*"May Allah disfigure the faces of Taghlib, whenever the pilgrims glorify and proclaim the greatness of God with proclamation."*

"The Most High" (al-aʿla) is an attribute of the Lord, and it has been said that it is an attribute of the name. The first is more preferable.

His saying: ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾ is another attribute of the Lord.

Al-Zajjaj said: He created man upright (mustawiyan), and the meaning of "proportioned" (sawwa) is that He made his stature balanced (ʿadala qamatahu).

Al-Dahhak said: He created him and proportioned his creation. It has been said: He created the bodies and proportioned the faculties of understanding. It has been said: He created man and prepared him for legal responsibility (al-taklif).

﴿And who determined and guided﴾ is another attribute of the Lord, or it is conjoined (maʿtuf) to the relative clause preceding it.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, al-Kisaʾi and al-Sulami read "qadar" (determined) with light stress, and the rest read it with the doubled letter (tashdid). Al-Wahidi said: The commentators said: He determined the creation of the male and the female among the animals, and He guided the male to the female, how he should mount her.

Mujahid said: He guided man to the path of good and evil, and to happiness and misery.

It was also related from him that he said regarding the meaning of the verse: He determined happiness and misery and guided to right guidance and error, and He guided the cattle to their pastures.

It has been said: He determined their provisions and sustenance, and guided them to their livelihoods if they are humans, and to their pastures if they are wild animals.

ʿAtaʾ said: For every creature there was appointed what sustains it, and He guided it to that.

It has been said: He created the benefits in things, and guided man to the way of extracting them from them.

Al-Suddi said: He determined the period of the fetus in the womb as nine months, or less or more, then He guided it to come out of the womb.

Al-Farraʾ said: That is, He determined and guided, and He misguided (aḍalla), so one of the two was mentioned and the other omitted. There are sayings concerning the interpretation of the verse other than what we have mentioned.

The preferable view is not to specify one individual or several individuals of what the words "determined" and "guided" apply to, unless there is evidence indicating it. In the absence of evidence, it is to be understood as applying to whatever the meaning of the two verbs covers, either by substitution (al-badal) or by comprehensiveness (al-shumul). The meaning is: He determined the kinds of things, their types, their attributes, their actions, their sayings and their terms, and He guided each one of them to what proceeds from it and what befits it, and He facilitated for it what it was created for, and He inspired it toward the affairs of its religion and its worldly life.

﴿And who brought forth the pasture﴾ is another attribute of the Lord: that is, He caused the herbage to grow, and the green plants which the cattle graze.

﴿Then made it dark stubble (ghuthaʾan aḥwa)﴾: that is, after it was green, He made it stubble (ghuthaʾ), that is, dry crumbled herbage like the debris that rides atop a flood. "Aḥwa" means black after its greenness, because when the herbage dries it turns black.

Qatadah said: "Ghuthaʾ" is dry matter. It is said of herbs and grass when they are broken and dried: ghuthaʾ and hashim.

Imru' al-Qays said:

*"As if the tops of the head of al-Mujaymir in the morning, from the flood and the debris, were a spindle-whorl."*

The accusative of "ghuthaʾan" is either as the second object, or as a circumstantial state (hal), and "aḥwa" is an attribute of it.

Al-Kisaʾi said: It is a state of "the pasture": that is, He brought it forth black from the intensity of its greenness and irrigation, then after that He made it stubble. "Aḥwa" is derived from "al-ḥuwwah," which is a blackness inclining toward green.

In al-Sihah it is said: "al-ḥuwwah" is the darkness of the lip, and from this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

*"Lamyaʾ (a woman with dark lips), in her lips is ḥuwwah of lʿas, and in her gums and in her canine teeth is shanab."*

﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾: that is, We shall make you a reciter, by inspiring you with recitation, so you will not forget what you recite. The sentence is resumptive (mustaʾnafah), to explain his ﷺ special guidance after the explanation of the general guidance, and it is his ﷺ guidance to memorize the Qur'an.

Mujahid and al-Kalbi said: "When Gabriel came down to the Prophet ﷺ with the revelation, Gabriel did not finish the last part of the verse before the Prophet ﷺ began speaking the first part of it, for fear that he would forget it. So ﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾ was revealed."

His saying: ﴿except what Allah wills﴾ is an exceptive (istithnaʾ mufarragh) from the most general of the objects: that is, you will not forget anything of what you recite except what Allah wills that you forget.

Al-Farraʾ said: He, glorified is He, did not will that Muhammad ﷺ forget anything, like His saying: ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾ [Hud: 107]. It has been said: "except what Allah wills" means that you forget, then you remember after that. So he forgets, but he remembers, and does not forget anything with a complete forgetting.

It has been said that it means naskh (abrogation), that is: except what Allah wills to abrogate its recitation.

It has been said that the meaning of ﴿so you will not forget﴾ is: so do not abandon acting upon it, except what Allah wills that you abandon, because of its abrogation and the lifting of its ruling.

It has been said that the meaning is: except what Allah wills to delay its sending down.

It has been said that the "lā" in His saying ﴿so you will not forget﴾ is a prohibition (lā al-nahy). The alif is added for the sake of the rhyme (fawasil), as in His saying: ﴿So they misled us from the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67]. The meaning is: do not neglect its recitation, and remember it.

﴿Indeed He knows the open and what is hidden﴾: this sentence is a justification (taʿlil) for what precedes it: that is, He knows what is manifest and what is concealed, and the public and the private. Its apparent meaning is generality, so there falls under it what has been said: that the "open" is what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ memorized of the Qur'an, and what is "hidden" is what was abrogated from his heart. Also falling under it is what has been said: that the open is the public declaration of charity, and what is hidden is concealing it. Also falling under it is what has been said: that the open is his ﷺ recitation of the Qur'an aloud along with Gabriel's recitation, for fear that it would slip from him, and what is hidden is what is in his soul of what calls him to speak aloud.
