This was mentioned to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said, 'O Messenger of God, I came to pray, and he prolonged it for me, so I left and prayed in a corner of the mosque, then I watered my camel.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, 'Are you a troublemaker, O Mu'adh? Where are you from ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [87:1], ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [91:1], ﴿By the dawn﴾, ﴿and by the night when it covers﴾ [92:1]?'"

In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

[p-1617] He, glorified is He, swore by these things, just as He swore by other of His creatures.

Opinion differs concerning the dawn by which God swears here. It is said it is the well-known time, and it was named *fajr* (dawn) because it is the time when darkness splits (*infijar*) from the day every day.

Qatadah said: it is the dawn of the first day of the month of Muharram, because the year bursts forth (*tatafajjaru*) from it.

Mujahid said: he means the Day of Sacrifice (*yawm al-nahr*).

Al-Dahhak said: the dawn of Dhu al-Hijjah.

This is because God linked the days with it, saying ﴿and ten nights﴾ [89:2], meaning ten nights of Dhu al-Hijjah. Al-Suddi and al-Kalbi also said this.

It is said that the meaning is: the prayer of dawn, or the Lord of the dawn.

The first is preferable.

The answer (*jawab*) to this oath and what follows it is His saying ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [89:14]. Thus Ibn al-Anbari said. It is also said that it is omitted, being indicated by the context: that is, ﴿He will surely reward every person according to what he did,﴾ or ﴿He will surely punish.﴾ Abu Hayyan estimated it as what is indicated by the end of the preceding surah: that is, "By the dawn, etc., for their return to Us and their reckoning by Us." This is very weak. Even weaker is the saying of the one who said the answer is His saying ﴿Is there in that an oath for one of intellect?﴾ [89:5], and that *hal* (is/does) here means *qad* (indeed). This is because that cannot ever be what is sworn to.

﴿and ten nights﴾ [89:2] are the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah according to the saying of the majority of the commentators.

Al-Dahhak said: they are the last (nights) of Ramadan. It is also said: the first ten of Muharram up to its tenth, the day of Ashura.

The majority read *layalin* with tanwin, and *'ashrin* is an adjective (*sifa*) of it.

Ibn Abbas read *wa-layali 'ashrin* with the idafa (construct). It is said the intended meaning is *layali ayyam 'ashr* (nights of ten days). According to this, its requirement would be to say *'ashara* (feminine form), because the counted noun is masculine.

It was answered that when the counted noun is omitted, both forms are permissible.

﴿and the even and the odd﴾ [89:3]. The even (*al-shaf'*) and the odd (*al-watr*) encompass all things, their even and their odd. It is also said: the even and odd nights.

Qatadah said: the even and the odd are the even and odd of the prayer; from it there is an even and from it there is an odd.

It is said: the even is the Day of Arafah and the Day of Sacrifice, and the odd is the night of the Day of Sacrifice.

Mujahid and Ata' al-Awfi said: the even is creation, and the odd is God, the One, the Eternal Refuge (*al-Samad*). Muhammad ibn Sirin, Masruq, Abu Salih, and Qatadah also said this.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Abu al-'Aliyah said: it is the Maghrib prayer, in which there are two rak'ahs, and the odd is the single rak'ah.

Al-Dahhak said: the even is the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah and the odd is the three days of Mina. Ata' also said this. It is said they are Adam and Eve, because Adam was odd, so he was made even with Eve.

It is said the even is the degrees of Paradise, which are eight, and the odd is the levels of Hell, which are seven. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said this.

It is said the even is al-Safa and al-Marwah, and the odd is the Ka'bah.

Muqatil said: the even is the days and nights, and the odd is the day after which there is no night, which is the Day of Resurrection.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: the odd is God, glorified is He, and He is also the even, because of His saying ﴿There is no secret conference of three but He is their fourth﴾ [58:7], and so on.

Al-Hasan said: what is meant by the even and the odd is the whole number, because number does not lack these two.

It is said the even is the Mosque of Mecca and the Mosque of Medina, and the odd is the Mosque of Jerusalem.

It is said the even is the Hajj *qiran* (combined pilgrimage), and the odd is *ifrad* (solo pilgrimage).

It is said the even is living beings because they are male and female, and the odd is inanimate matter.

It is said the even is what has been named, and the odd is what has not been named.

Nothing is hidden from you about the clear weakness and evident feebleness of most of these sayings, and about relying on the mere false opinion and the mistaken notion in specifying them.

What should be relied upon, and what it is necessary to adopt, is what the meaning of *shaf'* and *watr* in the language of the Arabs indicates. Both are well known and clear: *shaf'* among the Arabs is a pair, and *watr* is the single.

So the intended meaning of the verse is either the number itself, or what can be described as even or odd among the counted things.

When there is evidence specifying one of the counted things in the interpretation of this verse, then if the evidence indicates that it is itself what is intended and not other than it, that is so. If the evidence indicates that it is among what this verse encompasses, that does not prevent the verse from encompassing other things.

The majority read *wa-l-watr* with a fatha on the waw.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read it with a kasra on it, and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and his companions. Both are dialects. The fatha is the dialect of the Quraysh and the people of the Hijaz, and the kasra is the dialect of Tamim.

Al-Asma'i said: every single is *witr*, and the people of the Hijaz pronounce it with a fatha, saying *watr* for the single.

Yunus related from Ibn Kathir that he read with a fatha on the waw and a kasra on the ta', so it may be a third dialect, or he transferred the kasra of the *ra'* to the *ta'*, treating the connected reading as a pause.

﴿and the night when it passes﴾ [89:4]. The majority read *yasri* with the omission of the *ya'* both in connection and in pause, following the orthography of the Mushaf.

Nafi' and Abu 'Amr omit it in pause and affirm it in connection.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, and Ya'qub affirm it both in connection and in pause.

Al-Khalil said: the *ya'* drops from it in agreement with the ends of verses (*ru'us al-ayy*).

Al-Zajjaj said: the omission is more beloved to me, because it is a closing word (*fasila*), and the closing words have the *ya'* dropped from them.

Al-Farra' said: the Arabs may drop the *ya'* and be content with the kasra before it. Some of them recited:

*Kafaka kaffun ma taliqu dirhaman*
*judan wa-ukhra tu'ti bi-l-sayfi daman*

*Ma taliqu* means: what it holds.

Al-Mu'arrij said: I asked al-Akhfash about the reason for dropping the *ya'* from *yasri*, and he said: "I will not answer you until you spend a year sleeping at the door of my house." So he spent a year sleeping at the door of his house, and then he said: "The night does not travel; rather it is traveled in. It is turned away from its direction, and whatever you turn away from its direction, you deprive of its *i'rab* (case endings). Do you not see His saying ﴿and your mother was not unchaste﴾ [19:28], and He did not say *baghiyyah*, because He turned it from *baghiyah* (unchaste woman)."

There is a point to be considered in al-Akhfash's statement. Turning a thing away from its meaning for some reason does not necessitate turning its word away from some of what it deserves. If that were valid, it would apply to all rational and verbal metaphors (*al-majazat al-'aqliyya wa-l-lafziyya*), and the consequence is false, so the premise is likewise false. The basic principle here is the affirmation of the *ya'*, because it is the final radical of the imperfect verb in the nominative, and it was never dropped for any reason except following the orthography of the Mushaf and agreeing with the ends of verses, treating the closing words as rhyme (*qawafi*).

The meaning of ﴿and the night when it passes﴾ is "when it goes on," like His saying ﴿and the night when it turns back﴾ [74:33], and ﴿and the night when it withdraws﴾ [81:17]. It is also said the meaning of *yasri* is: there is traveling in it (*yasar fihi*), as it is said "a sleeping night" and "a fasting day." As in the verse of the poet:

*Laqad lumtina ya Umma Ghaylana fi al-suri*
*wa-nimti wa-ma layl al-matiyyi bi-na'imi*

Al-Akhfash, al-Qutaybi, and others among the people of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said this, while the majority of the commentators said the first.

Qatadah and Abu al-'Aliyah said: ﴿and the night when it passes﴾ means it came and approached.

Al-Nakha'i said: it means it stood still (*istawa*).

'Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Kalbi, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it is specifically the night of Muzdalifah, because of the gathering of people in it for obedience to God, glorified is He. It is also said it is the Night of Power (*laylat al-qadr*), because of the spreading of mercy in it.

The preponderant view is not to specify one night over the other nights.

﴿Is there in that an oath for one of intellect?﴾ [89:5]. This interrogation is for affirming the glorification and magnification of what God, glorified is He, swore by, from these mentioned matters. The indication by His saying "that" (*dhalika*) refers to those matters, and the masculine is by interpretation of "the mentioned" (*al-madhkur*), meaning: is there in that mentioned set of matters which We swore by an oath, i.e., a sworn-by thing deserving that reports be emphasized by it, ﴿for one of intellect (*hijr*)﴾, i.e., of reason and understanding. Whoever has reason and understanding knows that what God swore by of these things deserves to be sworn by. Similar to this is His saying ﴿And indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew﴾ [56:76].

Al-Hasan said: ﴿hijr﴾ means of forbearance (*hilm*).

Abu Malik said: of concealment (*sitr*) from people.

The majority said: *hijr* is reason ('aql).

Al-Farra' said: all of them return to one meaning: for one of reason, for one of forbearance, for one of concealment; all of them mean reason.

The root of *hijr* is prevention. It is said of one who has mastered himself and restrained it: "He is one of *hijr*." From it the stone (*hajar*) is named for its resistance through its hardness. From it: the judge *hajara* on so-and-so, i.e., prevented him.

He said: the Arabs say "he is one of *hijr*" when he is dominant over himself and controls it.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned by way of citation (*'ala tariqat al-istishhad*) what befell some groups of the disbelievers of His punishment due to their unbelief, obstinacy, and denial of the messengers, as a warning to the disbelievers in the era of our Prophet (ﷺ) and a frightening of them lest what befell them befall them. So He said:

﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with 'Ad, Iram of the pillars?﴾ [89:6–7]. The majority read *'Adin* with tanwin, with *Iram* as an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*) to *'Ad*. What is meant by *'Ad* is the name of their father, and *Iram* is the name of the tribe, or a substitute (*badal*) for it. Its not taking tanwin is due to definiteness and feminine gender.

It is also said that what is meant by *'Ad* is the sons of 'Ad, and they are the first 'Ad. The later ones are called the second 'Ad. So the mention of *Iram* is in the manner of explicative apposition or substitution, to indicate that they are the first 'Ad and not the second 'Ad. On both views an omitted noun must be assumed: that is, the people of Iram, or the lineage of Iram. This is because Iram is the grandfather of 'Ad, since he is 'Ad son of 'Ws son of Iram son of Sam son of Noah.

Al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliyah read *'Ad* in the idafa (construct) to *Iram*.

The majority read *Iram* with a kasra on the hamza, a fatha on the ra' and the mim.

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak read *Aram* with a fatha on the hamza and the ra'. Mu'adh read with a sukun on the ra' for lightness. It was also read with the idafa of *Iram* to *dhat al-'imad*.

Mujahid said: whoever reads with a fatha on the hamza likens them to the *aram*, which are the landmarks (*a'lam*), singular *aram*. In the speech there is inversion (*taqdim wa-ta'khir*): that is, "By the dawn, and such and such ... Indeed your Lord is ever watchful." "Have you not seen": i.e., has your knowledge not reached what your Lord did to 'Ad? This seeing is the seeing of the heart, and the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to whoever is suitable for it. The affair of 'Ad and Thamud was well known among the Arabs, because their dwellings were adjacent to the dwellings of the Arabs, and they used to hear from the People of the Book about the affair of Pharaoh.

Mujahid also said: Iram is a nation among the nations. Qatadah said: it is a tribe from 'Ad. It is also said they were two 'Ads: the first is Iram. From it is the saying of Qays ibn al-Ruqayyat:

*Majdan taliidan banahu awwaluhum*
*adraka 'Adan wa-qablahu Iram*

Ma'mar said: Iram is the gathering place of 'Ad and Thamud, and it used to be said "'Ad of Iram" and "'Ad of Thamud," and the two tribes were ascribed to Iram.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: they are two 'Ads, the first is Iram.

The meaning of ﴿dhat al-'imad﴾ [89:7]: possessors of strength and power, derived from the strength of pillars (*a'madah*). Al-Dahhak said this.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: they were people of mobile pillars (*'umud sayyara*) in the spring; when the plant grew, they returned to their dwellings.

Muqatil said: ﴿dhat al-'imad﴾ means their height. A man among them was twelve cubits tall. It is said: "a man of tall *'imad*," i.e., of stature.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: ﴿dhat al-'imad﴾ means possessors of height. It is said: "a *ra'j mu'ammad*" when it is tall.

Mujahid and Qatadah also said: he was a pillar (*'imad*) for their people. It is said: "So-and-so is the *'amid* of the people and their *'amud*," i.e., their chief.

Ibn Zayd said: ﴿dhat al-'imad﴾ means the firm construction of buildings with pillars.

Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: "al-'imad" means lofty buildings; it is used in both the masculine and feminine. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

"When the pillar of the tribe falls, we, on the low ground, protect whoever is near us."

'Ikrimah and Sa'id al-Maqburi said: it is Damascus. Ibn Wahb and Ashhab related this from Malik.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it is Alexandria.

﴿which had no like created in the lands﴾: this is a description of 'Ad, meaning that no tribe like them was created in height, strength and power. These are the ones who said: ﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾ [Fussilat: 15]. Or it is a description of the city, according to those who said that Iram is the name of their city or of the land in which they lived.

The first is preferable, and the reading of Ubayy supports it: "which had no like of them created in the lands." It was also said that Iram means destruction.

Al-Dahhak said regarding ﴿Iram, of the pillars﴾: that He destroyed them and made them crumbled remains. Shahr ibn Hawshab also said this.

A group of exegetes mentioned that ﴿Iram, of the pillars﴾ is the name of a city built of gold and silver, its palaces, houses and gardens included, its pebbles are jewels and its dust is musk. No one lives there and no child of Adam dwells in it, and it keeps moving from place to place: sometimes it is in Yemen, sometimes in Syria, sometimes in Iraq, and sometimes in other lands. This is pure falsehood, which does not pass for anyone with even minimal discernment.

al-Tha'labi added in his tafsir, saying that 'Abd Allah ibn Qilabah entered this city in the time of Mu'awiyah. This is a lie upon a lie and a fabrication upon a fabrication. Islam and its people have been struck by a grave calamity, a great disaster and a immense tragedy, from liars and deceivers of this kind who dare to lie: sometimes about the Children of Israel, sometimes about the prophets, sometimes about the righteous, and sometimes about the Lord of the worlds. This evil has multiplied and grown greater because of groups of people who have no knowledge of sound narration from weak, or fabricated, and who take up authorship and exegesis of the Mighty Book. They introduced these fabricated superstitions, invented stories and forged legends into the tafsir of the Book of Allah, Glorified is He, so they distorted, altered and changed.

Whoever wishes to become acquainted with some of what we have mentioned should look into my book which I named al-Fawa'id al-Majmu'ah fi al-Ahadith al-Mawdu'ah (The Collected Benefits concerning Fabricated Hadith).

Then He, Glorified is He, linked the other tribe, Thamud, to the tribe of 'Ad, saying: ﴿And Thamud, who hewed out the rocks in the valley﴾. They are the people of Salih, named after their forefather Thamud ibn 'Abir ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh. The meaning of ﴿hewed out the rocks﴾ is cut them; al-jawb means cutting, and from it comes "jaba al-bilad" when one crosses the lands, and from it the collar of a shirt (jayb al-qamis) is so named because it is a cut, i.e., an opening.

The exegetes said: Thamud were the first to carve mountains and rocks, and they built from stone 1,700 cities. From this is His saying: ﴿And they carved houses out of the mountains, secure﴾ [al-Hijr: 82]. They used to carve the mountains, hollow them out, and make those hollows into dwellings in which they lived. His saying "in the valley" is connected to "hewed out," or to an omitted element, as a circumstantial clause describing the rock. It is the Valley of al-Qura.

The majority read Thamud without tanwin, as the name of the tribe, which carries the features of feminine gender and definiteness. Yahya ibn Wuthab read it with tanwin, as the name of their forefather. The majority also read "bi-l-wad" with the ya' omitted both in connected speech and at pause, following the orthography of the Mushaf. Ibn Kathir read it with the ya' affirmed in both cases. Qunbul, in one narration from him, affirmed it in connected speech but not at pause.

﴿And Pharaoh of the stakes﴾: that is, the possessor of armies who had many tents that they fastened with stakes; or the armies themselves were made into stakes, because they support the king as stakes support tents. It was also said that he had stakes with which he tortured people and fastened them to them. The explanation of this has already been given in Surat Sad.

﴿Who transgressed in the lands﴾: the relative clause describes 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh. That is, each group among them transgressed in its lands, rebelled and was insolent. Transgression is going beyond the limit.

﴿So they multiplied corruption therein﴾ through disbelief, disobedience to Allah and oppression of His servants. The relative clause may also be in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are those who transgressed," or in the accusative position by way of dispraise.

﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾: that is, He poured out and cast upon those groups a scourge of punishment, which is what He punished them with.

al-Zajjaj said: He made the whip with which He struck them into punishment. It is said: "sabba 'ala fulan khul'ah," meaning he cast a robe upon him. From this is the saying of al-Nabighah:

"So Allah cast upon him the finest dye, and he had among the creation a helper."

From it also is the saying of another:

"Do you not see that Allah made His religion manifest, and poured upon the disbelievers a scourge of punishment?"

The meaning of ﴿scourge of punishment﴾ is a portion of punishment. The mention of the whip indicates that the great punishment He inflicted on them in this world is, compared with what He has prepared for them in the Hereafter, like a whip compared with all other means of punishment.

It was also said that the mention of the whip serves to indicate the severity of what befell them, for the whip was, among them, the extreme of punishment.

al-Farra' said: it is a word the Arabs use for every kind of punishment. The origin of this is that the whip was the punishment they used to torture with, so it became applied to every punishment whose extreme is among them.

It was also said its meaning is: a punishment that mixes with flesh and blood, from the expression "sawwata yasuwwatuhu sawtan", meaning he mixed it. So "sawt" is mixing one thing with another. From it is the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

"But a friendship whose blood was mixed with grief, betrayal, breaking of promises and change."

And another said:

"O Harith, if our bloods were mixed, they would be separated until no blood touches blood."

And another said:

"So mix him, blameworthy in judgment and unsuccessful, for you are not one who helps in mixing him."

﴿Indeed your Lord is ever in observation﴾: We have already mentioned the view of those who said that this is the answer to the oath. The more preferable view is that the answer is omitted, and this sentence is an explanation of what precedes it. It contains guidance that the disbelievers among his people, the Prophet (ﷺ)'s people, will suffer what befell those disbelievers. The meaning of "bil-mirsad" is that He watches the deeds of every person until He recompenses him for it, good with good and evil with evil.

Al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah said: that is, the path of the servants is under His control, and none escapes Him. Al-rasd and al-mirsad mean "the road."

Its explanation has already been given in Surat Bara'ah, and it was also mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿Indeed, Hell was a place of ambush﴾ [al-Naba': 21].

al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿By the dawn﴾ that he said: the dawn of the day.

Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: it means the dawn prayer.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab and Ibn 'Asakir related from him, also regarding ﴿By the dawn﴾, that he said: it is the month of Muharram, the dawn of the year. Authentic hadiths have been reported concerning the virtue of fasting in the month of Muharram, but they do not indicate that it is what is meant by the verse, neither by direct correspondence, nor by implication, nor by necessary inference.

Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from Jabir that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "﴿By the dawn, and ten nights, and the even and the odd﴾: the ten are the ten of al-Adha, the odd is the Day of 'Arafah, and the even is the Day of Sacrifice."

In another wording: they are nights of Dhu al-Hijjah.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Talhah ibn 'Abd Allah that he entered upon Ibn 'Umar together with Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, and Ibn 'Umar invited them to lunch on the Day of 'Arafah. Abu Salamah said: Are these not the ten nights that Allah mentioned in the Qur'an? Ibn 'Umar said: And how would you know? He said: I have no doubt. He said: Then doubt.

Hadiths have been reported concerning the virtue of these ten, but there is nothing in them that indicates they are what is meant by the Qur'anic mention here in any way.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And ten nights﴾ that he said: they are the last ten of Ramadan.

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim (who graded it sound) and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Imran ibn Husayn that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the even and the odd, and he said: it is the prayer, some of it is even and some of it is odd." In its chain there is an unknown man, and he is the one who narrated it from 'Imran ibn Husayn.

It has also been narrated from 'Imran ibn 'Isam from 'Imran ibn Husayn without the unknown man.

al-Tirmidhi said after reporting it with the chain containing the unknown man: "It is a gharib hadith which we do not know except through the narration of Qatadah."

Ibn Kathir said: In my view its being a statement of 'Imran ibn Husayn is more likely, and Allah knows best.

He said: Ibn Jarir did not decide on any of these views concerning the even and the odd.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related this hadith as a statement of 'Imran ibn Husayn, and this strengthens what Ibn Kathir said.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿By the even and the odd﴾ that he said: everything is even or it is two, and the odd is one.

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh, as al-Suyuti said with a weak chain, related from Abu Ayyub from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he was asked about the even and the odd and said: "Two days and a night: the Day of 'Arafah and the Day of Sacrifice; and the odd is the night of Sacrifice, the night of gathering."

Ibn Jarir related from Jabir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The even is the two days, and the odd is the third day."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Sa'd, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that he was asked about the even and the odd and said: the even is Allah's saying: ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203], and the odd is the third day.

In another wording: the odd is the middle of the days of Tashriq.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the even is the Day of Sacrifice, and the odd is the Day of 'Arafah.

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding ﴿And the night when it passes﴾ that he said: when it departs.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited ﴿By the dawn﴾ up to His saying ﴿when it passes﴾ and said: this is an oath upon ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever in observation﴾.

al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿an oath for one who has intellect﴾ that he said: for one who has reason, intellect and understanding.

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding His saying ﴿Iram, with the pillars﴾ that he said: by Iram he means the destroyed; do you not see that you say "the people of so-and-so were destroyed (urima)"? ﴿of the pillars﴾: he means their height was like the pillar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from al-Miqdam ibn Ma'di Karib that "the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned ﴿Iram, of the pillars﴾ and said: a man among them would come to a rock, lift it upon his shoulder, and throw it upon whatever tribe he wished, and destroy them."

In its chain there is an unknown man, because Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated it from one who narrated to him from al-Miqdam.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿who hewed out the rocks in the valley﴾ that he said: they split them.

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding the verse that he said: they used to carve houses out of the mountains. ﴿And Pharaoh of the stakes﴾: he said: the stakes are the armies who fastened his affairs for him.

al-Hakim (who graded it sound) related from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying ﴿of the stakes﴾ that he said: Pharaoh staked his wife to four stakes, then placed upon her back a great millstone until she died.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever in observation﴾ that he said: He hears and He sees.

Al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat (The Names and Attributes), narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾. He said: "Beyond the Sirat (the bridge over Hell) are bridges: a bridge on which is trust (al-amanah), a bridge on which are the ties of kinship (al-rahim), and a bridge on which is the Lord, Mighty and Majestic."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 89, verses 15–30 (part 1 of 2):

When the Exalted mentioned that He is ever watchful (bi-l-mirsad), He mentioned what indicates the variation in His servants' conditions upon receiving good and upon receiving evil, and that the object of their gaze and the greatest of their aims is this world. So He said: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him﴾, meaning He tries and examines him with blessings, ﴿and honors him and bestows favor upon him﴾, meaning He honors him with wealth and widens his provision. ﴿Then he says, "My Lord has honored me,"﴾ rejoicing in what he has attained and delighted in what he has been given, not thankful to God for it, and not considering that this is a trial from his Lord, a test of his state and a disclosure of what he harbors of patience, impatience, gratitude for the blessing, or ingratitude for it. The "mā" in His words "idhā mā" is superfluous (zā'idah). His words ﴿and honors him and bestows favor upon him﴾ are an explanation of the "testing." The meaning of "akramanī" is: He has favored me with the wealth He has given me and lavished blessings upon me, because I deserve it more and because I am its appropriate recipient. "Al-insān" is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "fa-yaqūlu rabbī akramanī." The "fa" entered into it because "amma" (as for) carries the sense of a conditional. The adverbial phrase placed between the subject and the predicate, although it precedes in wording, is delayed in meaning. That is: "As for man, then he says, 'My Lord has honored me,' at the time of his being tested with favors."

Al-Kalbi said: "al-Insān" is the disbeliever, Ubayy ibn Khalaf.

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Umayya ibn Khalaf. It was also said it was revealed concerning Utba ibn Rabi'a and Abu Hudhayfa ibn al-Mughira.

﴿But as for when He tests him﴾, meaning He examines him and treats him as one who is being examined, ﴿and so restricts his provision for him﴾, meaning He constricts it and does not widen it for him nor extends it to him. ﴿Then he says, "My Lord has humiliated me,"﴾ meaning He has assigned him humiliation. This is the attribute of the disbeliever who does not believe in the Resurrection, for to him there is no honor except the world and the widening of its enjoyments, and there is no humiliation to him except losing them and failing to reach what he desires of its adornments. As for the believer, honor for him is that God honors him by his obedience and enables him to perform the works of the Hereafter. It is possible that "al-insān" is intended in a general sense, because of his lack of certainty that what came to him of good in this world and what befell him of evil are nothing but a test and an examination, and that the whole world is not worth, in the sight of God, the wing of a mosquito. Had it been worth the wing of a mosquito, He would not have given the disbeliever a single sip of water from it.

Nāfi' recited with the ya' (the final long vowel) affirmed in "akramanī" and "ahānanī" when connected, and omitted them when pausing. Ibn Kathīr, in the transmission of al-Bazzī from him, and Ibn Muḥaysin, and Ya'qūb recited with both affirmed, both in connection and in pause. The rest recited with both omitted in connection and in pause, following the orthography of the Muṣḥaf (the written codex) and for conformity with the ends of verses (ru'ūs al-āy). The original form is with them affirmed, since it is a noun (ism). Among the omission is the poet's verse:

"And from an enemy whose hidden rancor is apparent, when I stand before him, he disowned me (ankaranī)."

That is, "ankaranī" (he disowned me).

Al-Jumhūr recited "fa-qadara" with the light form (takhfīf), and Ibn 'Āmir recited it with the doubled form (tashdīd), and both are dialects.

Al-Ḥaramayn (Ibn Kathīr and Nāfi') and Abū 'Amr recited "rabbī" with a fatḥa on the ya' in both places, and the rest recited it with sukūn.

His words "kallā" (no indeed) are a deterrent to man who said what he said in both states, and a rebuke to him. For God, the Exalted, may widen provision and extend blessings to a person, not as a sign of his honor, and He may constrict it for him, not as a sign of his humiliation, but for testing and examination, as has preceded.

Al-Farrā' said: "Kallā" in this place means: it was not fitting for the servant to be in this condition, but rather he should praise God for wealth and for poverty.

Then the Exalted moved from describing the evil of man's words to describing the evil of his deeds, and so He said: ﴿Nay, you do not honor the orphan﴾. The turn to direct address (al-iltifāt ilā al-khiṭāb) is for the purpose of reproach and censure, according to the recitation of the majority with the second-person form (al-fawqiyyah).

Al-Jumhūr recited "taḥāḍḍūna," "ta'kulūna," and "tuḥibbūna" with the second-person form (al-fawqiyyah) for address in them.

Abū 'Amr and Ya'qūb recited them with the third-person form (al-taḥtiyyah). The plural in these verbs is in view of the meaning of "al-insān," because what is meant by it is the category. That is: "Nay, you have deeds that are uglier than what has been mentioned, namely that you abandon honoring the orphan, so you eat his wealth and withhold from him the surplus of your own wealth."

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Qudāma ibn Maẓ'ūn, who was an orphan in the custody of Umayya ibn Khalaf.

﴿And you do not urge one another to feed the needy﴾. Al-Jumhūr recited "tuḥḍḍūna," from "ḥaddahu 'alā kadhā," meaning he incited him to it, and its object is omitted: that is, "you do not urge yourselves," or "none of you urges another to that, nor commands it, nor guides to it." The Kufans recited "tataḥāḍḍūna" with a fatḥa on the tā' and an alif after the ḥā', and its origin is "tataḥāḍḍūna," so one of the two tā's is dropped: that is, "none of you urges another."

Al-Kisā'ī in one of the transmissions from him, and al-Sulamī, recited "tuḥāḍḍūna" with a ḍamma on the tā', from al-ḥaḍḍ, which is urging. His words ﴿on the feeding of the needy﴾ are related to "tuḥḍḍūna." It is either a verbal noun (ism maṣdar), meaning "on feeding the needy," or a noun for the food, and it would then be with an elided modifier (ḥadhf muḍāf), meaning "on giving out the food of the needy," or "on giving the food of the needy."

﴿And you devour the inheritance﴾. Its origin is "al-wurāth," so the tā' was substituted for a ḍammed wāw, as in "tujāh" and "wijāh." What is meant by it is the wealth of orphans who inherit it from their relatives, and likewise the wealth of women. That is because they used not to give inheritance to women and children, and they would consume their wealth ﴿with greedy devouring﴾, meaning intense devouring. It was also said the meaning of "lamman" is gathering, from the saying: "lamamtu al-ṭa'ām," when you ate all of it.

Al-Ḥasan said: He eats his own share and the share of the orphan. Abū 'Ubayda said likewise.

The original meaning of "al-lamm" in Arabic speech is gathering. It is said: "lamamtu al-shay' alummuhu lamman," meaning I gathered it. From this is the saying: "lamma Allāh sha'athahu," meaning God gathered what had scattered of his affairs. From this is the verse of al-Nābigha:

"You are not one who would leave behind a brother whom you do not gather up, despite his disorder; which of men is refined?"

Al-Layth said: "al-lamm" is intense gathering, and from it come "ḥajar malmūm" (a gathered stone) and "katība malmūma" (a gathered army). The one who eats "yalummu al-tharīd," meaning he gathers the bread-and-broth and then eats it.

Mujāhid said: He lap it up (yasiffuhu saffan).

Ibn Zayd said: When he has consumed his own wealth, he gathers together the wealth of others and eats it, without considering what he has eaten of the foul and the good.

﴿And you love wealth with abundant love﴾, meaning intense love. "Al-jamm" is the abundant. It is said: "jamma al-mā' fī al-ḥawḍ," when the water increased and gathered. "Al-jamma" is the place where water gathers.

Then the Exalted repeated the deterrent and rebuke to them, and said: "Kallā," meaning this is not how your deeds should be.

Then the Exalted began anew, and said: ﴿When the earth is ground to powder, grinding upon grinding﴾. In this is a warning to them after the deterrent and rebuke. "Al-dakk" is breaking and crushing. The meaning here: it was shaken and moved with a movement after a movement.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Its mountains were crushed until they became level.

Al-Zajjāj said: That is, it was shaken and so some of it crushed others.

Al-Mubarrad said: That is, it was spread out and its elevation disappeared. He said: "al-dakk" is bringing down the elevated by flattening. The discussion of "al-dakk" has already preceded in the surah al-A'rāf and in the surah al-Aḥqāf. The meaning: it was crushed once after another. The accusative of the first "dakkan" is as a verbal noun emphasizing the verb, and the second "dakkan" is an emphasis of the first, so said Ibn 'Uṣfūr.

It is permissible that the accusative is as a circumstantial (ḥāl), meaning in the state of being crushed time after time, as one says: "I taught him arithmetic chapter by chapter (bāban bāban), and I taught him the script letter by letter (ḥarfan ḥarfan)." The meaning: He repeated the crushing upon it until it became scattered dust (habā'an munbaththan).

﴿And your Lord comes﴾, meaning His command and His decree comes, and His signs appear. It was also said the meaning is: the doubts on that day cease, and the realities become manifest and necessary, as doubt vanishes upon the arrival of the thing that was being doubted. It was also said: the subjugation of your Lord, His authority, and His sole control of the command and governance comes, without giving anyone of His servants any part of that. ﴿And the angels, rank upon rank﴾. The accusative of "ṣaffan ṣaffan" is as a circumstantial: that is, "lined up," or "possessors of rows."

'Aṭā' said: He means the rows of angels, and the people of each heaven are a separate row.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The people of each heaven, when they descend on the Day of Resurrection, will be a row encircling the earth and those upon it, so they will be seven rows.

﴿And Hell will be brought on that day﴾. "Yawma'idhin" is in the accusative governed by "jī'a." The one standing in place of the subject is "bi-Jahannam." Makkī permitted that "yawma'idhin" be the one standing in place of the subject, but that is not right.

Al-Wāḥidī said: A group of the exegetes said: It will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, bridled with seventy thousand bridles, with each bridle having seventy thousand angels dragging it, until it is placed on the left side of the Throne. No angel brought near, nor prophet sent, will remain without falling to his knees, saying: "O Lord, myself! myself!"

This which he transmitted from a group of exegetes will come, God willing, traced back to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

﴿On that day man will remember﴾. "Yawma'idhin" here is a substitute for the "yawma'idhin" preceding it, meaning: on the day Hell is brought, man will remember.

That is, he will take admonition, recall what he neglected, and regret what he sent ahead of himself in the world of disbelief and sins.

It was also said that the second "yawma'idhin" is a substitute for the phrase "idhā dukkat," and that the governing element for both is His words "yatadhakkaru al-insān."

﴿But how will the remembrance benefit him?﴾, meaning from where will he have remembrance and admonition? It was also said it is with an elided modifier: that is, from where will he have the benefit of the remembrance?

Al-Zajjāj said: He shows repentance, but from where is repentance?

﴿He will say, "Would that I had sent ahead for my life!"﴾ The sentence is a resumptive answer to an implied question, as if it was said: What will man say? It is also permissible that it is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) for His words "yatadhakkaru." The meaning: he wishes that he had sent ahead good and righteous deeds. The "lām" in "li-ḥayātī" means "for the sake of my life." What is meant is the life of the Hereafter, for it is the life in reality, because it is everlasting and not cut off.

It was also said that the "lām" means "in," and what is meant is the life of this world: that is, "Would that I had sent ahead righteous deeds during my life in the world, so that I might benefit from them this day." The first is preferable.

Al-Ḥasan said: By God, he knew that he had encountered a long life in which there is no death.

﴿So on that day none will punish as He punishes﴾, meaning on the day when the time of what has been mentioned of these conditions is, none will punish as God punishes. ﴿Nor will anyone bind as He binds﴾, or: none other than Him will undertake the punishment of God and His binding, since the whole matter belongs to Him. The two pronouns in both interpretations, in "'adhābihi" and "wathāqihi," refer to God, the Mighty and Majestic. This is according to the recitation of the majority, "yu'adhdhibu" and "yūthiqu," both in the active voice.

Al-Kisā'ī recited both in the passive voice, so the two pronouns refer back to man: that is, none will be punished with the punishment of that man, and none will be bound with his binding. "Al-insān" here means the disbeliever: that is, none who is not a disbeliever will be punished with the punishment of the disbeliever. It was also said it means Iblīs, and it was said it means Ubayy ibn Khalaf.

Al-Farrā' said: The meaning is that none will punish with the punishment of this specific disbeliever, nor bind with chains and shackles as he is bound, because of his extreme disbelief and obstinacy.

It was also said the meaning is: none will be punished in his place, and none will be bound in his place, so no ransom will be taken from him. This is like His words: ﴿And no bearer of burden shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'ām: 164]. "Al-'adhāb" is with the meaning of the punishing, and "al-wathāq" with the meaning of the binding.

Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred the recitation of al-Kisā'ī. He said: The pronoun in both places would be the pronoun of the disbeliever, since it is known that none punishes as God punishes.

Abū 'Alī al-Fārisī said: It is permissible that the pronoun refers to the disbeliever according to the recitation of the majority: that is, none punishes anyone as this disbeliever is punished.

When the Exalted finished relating the conditions of the wretched, He mentioned some conditions of the blessed, and so He said: ﴿O soul at peace﴾. "Al-muṭma'innah" is the one who is tranquil and certain in faith and in the oneness of God, who has reached the coolness of certainty (thalj al-yaqīn), such that no doubt mixes with it and no suspicion afflicts it.

Al-Ḥasan said: She is the believer who is certain.

Mujāhid said: She is the one content with God's decree, who knows that what missed her would never have been destined to reach her, and that what reached her would never have been destined to miss her.

Muqātil said: She is the safe and reassured one.

Ibn Kaysan said: "The tranquil soul" (al-mutma'innah) is the one at peace through the remembrance of God. It was also said: "the sincere one" (al-mukhlisah). Ibn Zayd said: it is called "the tranquil" because it was given the good news of Paradise at death and at the Resurrection.

﴿Return to your Lord﴾: that is, return to God, well-pleased with the reward He has given you, and well-pleasing in His sight. It was also said: return to His promise; and it was said: return to His command.

ʿIkrimah and ʿAta' said: the meaning of ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ is: return to your body in which you were. Ibn Jarir chose this view, and what supports it is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, "fa-odkhuli fi ʿabdi" (in the singular). The first view is preferable.

﴿Enter among My servants﴾: that is, among the company of My righteous servants; be one of them and join their ranks.

﴿And enter My Paradise﴾ along with them. It was said that she will be told "Return to your Lord" when she departs from this world, and she will be told "Enter among My servants and enter My Paradise" on the Day of Resurrection. The verse is meant in its general sense for every tranquil soul, and its revelation concerning a specific person does not preclude this; the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿eating (the inheritance) greedily (aklan lamma)﴾, that he said: "sweeping (safF)". And regarding His words ﴿love of wealth, immensely (hubban jamma)﴾, he said: "intensely." Ibn Jarir related from him also: ﴿aklan lamma﴾, he said: "intensely."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, regarding His words ﴿when the earth is leveled, leveled and leveled (dakkan dakka)﴾, that he said: "its shaking."

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "On that Day Hell will be brought forth, having seventy thousand bridles, with every bridle seventy thousand angels pulling it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿and how can he have the remembrance (wa-anna lahu al-dhikra)﴾ that he said: "And how could he?" Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His words ﴿on that Day none will punish as He punishes﴾ the verse, he said: "None will punish with the punishment of God, and none will bind with the bond of God."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from him also, regarding His words ﴿O tranquil soul﴾, he said: "the believing soul." ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ means: to your body.

He said: This verse was revealed while Abu Bakr was sitting, and he said: "O Messenger of God, how beautiful this is!" He said: "As for her, she will be told this."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nuʿaym in al-Hilyah related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr something similar, as a mursal report.

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul related something similar from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿O tranquil soul﴾ that it means "the one who affirms (the truth)."

Ibn Jarir related from him also regarding the verse that he said: "Souls will be returned to bodies on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding His words ﴿Return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ that he said: "with what she was given of reward, being well-pleased with her by her deeds." ﴿Enter among My servants﴾ means: the believers.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he said: Ibn ʿAbbas died at al-Ta'if, and a bird came, of a form not seen before, and entered his bier, and then it was not seen coming out of it. When he was buried, this verse was recited at the edge of the grave, and we do not know who recited it: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing, enter among My servants, and enter My Paradise.﴾

Abu Nuʿaym in al-Dala'il related something similar from ʿIkrimah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 89, verses 15–30 (part 1 of 2):

When the Exalted mentioned that He is ever watchful (bi-l-mirsad), He mentioned what indicates the variation in His servants' conditions upon receiving good and upon receiving evil, and that the object of their gaze and the greatest of their aims is this world. So He said: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him﴾, meaning He tries and examines him with blessings, ﴿and honors him and bestows favor upon him﴾, meaning He honors him with wealth and widens his provision. ﴿Then he says, "My Lord has honored me,"﴾ rejoicing in what he has attained and delighted in what he has been given, not thankful to God for it, and not considering that this is a trial from his Lord, a test of his state and a disclosure of what he harbors of patience, impatience, gratitude for the blessing, or ingratitude for it. The "mā" in His words "idhā mā" is superfluous (zā'idah). His words ﴿and honors him and bestows favor upon him﴾ are an explanation of the "testing." The meaning of "akramanī" is: He has favored me with the wealth He has given me and lavished blessings upon me, because I deserve it more and because I am its appropriate recipient. "Al-insān" is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "fa-yaqūlu rabbī akramanī." The "fa" entered into it because "amma" (as for) carries the sense of a conditional. The adverbial phrase placed between the subject and the predicate, although it precedes in wording, is delayed in meaning. That is: "As for man, then he says, 'My Lord has honored me,' at the time of his being tested with favors."

Al-Kalbi said: "al-Insān" is the disbeliever, Ubayy ibn Khalaf.

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Umayya ibn Khalaf. It was also said it was revealed concerning Utba ibn Rabi'a and Abu Hudhayfa ibn al-Mughira.

﴿But as for when He tests him﴾, meaning He examines him and treats him as one who is being examined, ﴿and so restricts his provision for him﴾, meaning He constricts it and does not widen it for him nor extends it to him. ﴿Then he says, "My Lord has humiliated me,"﴾ meaning He has assigned him humiliation. This is the attribute of the disbeliever who does not believe in the Resurrection, for to him there is no honor except the world and the widening of its enjoyments, and there is no humiliation to him except losing them and failing to reach what he desires of its adornments. As for the believer, honor for him is that God honors him by his obedience and enables him to perform the works of the Hereafter. It is possible that "al-insān" is intended in a general sense, because of his lack of certainty that what came to him of good in this world and what befell him of evil are nothing but a test and an examination, and that the whole world is not worth, in the sight of God, the wing of a mosquito. Had it been worth the wing of a mosquito, He would not have given the disbeliever a single sip of water from it.

Nāfi' recited with the ya' (the final long vowel) affirmed in "akramanī" and "ahānanī" when connected, and omitted them when pausing. Ibn Kathīr, in the transmission of al-Bazzī from him, and Ibn Muḥaysin, and Ya'qūb recited with both affirmed, both in connection and in pause. The rest recited with both omitted in connection and in pause, following the orthography of the Muṣḥaf (the written codex) and for conformity with the ends of verses (ru'ūs al-āy). The original form is with them affirmed, since it is a noun (ism). Among the omission is the poet's verse:

"And from an enemy whose hidden rancor is apparent, when I stand before him, he disowned me (ankaranī)."

That is, "ankaranī" (he disowned me).

Al-Jumhūr recited "fa-qadara" with the light form (takhfīf), and Ibn 'Āmir recited it with the doubled form (tashdīd), and both are dialects.

Al-Ḥaramayn (Ibn Kathīr and Nāfi') and Abū 'Amr recited "rabbī" with a fatḥa on the ya' in both places, and the rest recited it with sukūn.

His words "kallā" (no indeed) are a deterrent to man who said what he said in both states, and a rebuke to him. For God, the Exalted, may widen provision and extend blessings to a person, not as a sign of his honor, and He may constrict it for him, not as a sign of his humiliation, but for testing and examination, as has preceded.

Al-Farrā' said: "Kallā" in this place means: it was not fitting for the servant to be in this condition, but rather he should praise God for wealth and for poverty.

Then the Exalted moved from describing the evil of man's words to describing the evil of his deeds, and so He said: ﴿Nay, you do not honor the orphan﴾. The turn to direct address (al-iltifāt ilā al-khiṭāb) is for the purpose of reproach and censure, according to the recitation of the majority with the second-person form (al-fawqiyyah).

Al-Jumhūr recited "taḥāḍḍūna," "ta'kulūna," and "tuḥibbūna" with the second-person form (al-fawqiyyah) for address in them.

Abū 'Amr and Ya'qūb recited them with the third-person form (al-taḥtiyyah). The plural in these verbs is in view of the meaning of "al-insān," because what is meant by it is the category. That is: "Nay, you have deeds that are uglier than what has been mentioned, namely that you abandon honoring the orphan, so you eat his wealth and withhold from him the surplus of your own wealth."

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Qudāma ibn Maẓ'ūn, who was an orphan in the custody of Umayya ibn Khalaf.

﴿And you do not urge one another to feed the needy﴾. Al-Jumhūr recited "tuḥḍḍūna," from "ḥaddahu 'alā kadhā," meaning he incited him to it, and its object is omitted: that is, "you do not urge yourselves," or "none of you urges another to that, nor commands it, nor guides to it." The Kufans recited "tataḥāḍḍūna" with a fatḥa on the tā' and an alif after the ḥā', and its origin is "tataḥāḍḍūna," so one of the two tā's is dropped: that is, "none of you urges another."

Al-Kisā'ī in one of the transmissions from him, and al-Sulamī, recited "tuḥāḍḍūna" with a ḍamma on the tā', from al-ḥaḍḍ, which is urging. His words ﴿on the feeding of the needy﴾ are related to "tuḥḍḍūna." It is either a verbal noun (ism maṣdar), meaning "on feeding the needy," or a noun for the food, and it would then be with an elided modifier (ḥadhf muḍāf), meaning "on giving out the food of the needy," or "on giving the food of the needy."

﴿And you devour the inheritance﴾. Its origin is "al-wurāth," so the tā' was substituted for a ḍammed wāw, as in "tujāh" and "wijāh." What is meant by it is the wealth of orphans who inherit it from their relatives, and likewise the wealth of women. That is because they used not to give inheritance to women and children, and they would consume their wealth ﴿with greedy devouring﴾, meaning intense devouring. It was also said the meaning of "lamman" is gathering, from the saying: "lamamtu al-ṭa'ām," when you ate all of it.

Al-Ḥasan said: He eats his own share and the share of the orphan. Abū 'Ubayda said likewise.

The original meaning of "al-lamm" in Arabic speech is gathering. It is said: "lamamtu al-shay' alummuhu lamman," meaning I gathered it. From this is the saying: "lamma Allāh sha'athahu," meaning God gathered what had scattered of his affairs. From this is the verse of al-Nābigha:

"You are not one who would leave behind a brother whom you do not gather up, despite his disorder; which of men is refined?"

Al-Layth said: "al-lamm" is intense gathering, and from it come "ḥajar malmūm" (a gathered stone) and "katība malmūma" (a gathered army). The one who eats "yalummu al-tharīd," meaning he gathers the bread-and-broth and then eats it.

Mujāhid said: He lap it up (yasiffuhu saffan).

Ibn Zayd said: When he has consumed his own wealth, he gathers together the wealth of others and eats it, without considering what he has eaten of the foul and the good.

﴿And you love wealth with abundant love﴾, meaning intense love. "Al-jamm" is the abundant. It is said: "jamma al-mā' fī al-ḥawḍ," when the water increased and gathered. "Al-jamma" is the place where water gathers.

Then the Exalted repeated the deterrent and rebuke to them, and said: "Kallā," meaning this is not how your deeds should be.

Then the Exalted began anew, and said: ﴿When the earth is ground to powder, grinding upon grinding﴾. In this is a warning to them after the deterrent and rebuke. "Al-dakk" is breaking and crushing. The meaning here: it was shaken and moved with a movement after a movement.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Its mountains were crushed until they became level.

Al-Zajjāj said: That is, it was shaken and so some of it crushed others.

Al-Mubarrad said: That is, it was spread out and its elevation disappeared. He said: "al-dakk" is bringing down the elevated by flattening. The discussion of "al-dakk" has already preceded in the surah al-A'rāf and in the surah al-Aḥqāf. The meaning: it was crushed once after another. The accusative of the first "dakkan" is as a verbal noun emphasizing the verb, and the second "dakkan" is an emphasis of the first, so said Ibn 'Uṣfūr.

It is permissible that the accusative is as a circumstantial (ḥāl), meaning in the state of being crushed time after time, as one says: "I taught him arithmetic chapter by chapter (bāban bāban), and I taught him the script letter by letter (ḥarfan ḥarfan)." The meaning: He repeated the crushing upon it until it became scattered dust (habā'an munbaththan).

﴿And your Lord comes﴾, meaning His command and His decree comes, and His signs appear. It was also said the meaning is: the doubts on that day cease, and the realities become manifest and necessary, as doubt vanishes upon the arrival of the thing that was being doubted. It was also said: the subjugation of your Lord, His authority, and His sole control of the command and governance comes, without giving anyone of His servants any part of that. ﴿And the angels, rank upon rank﴾. The accusative of "ṣaffan ṣaffan" is as a circumstantial: that is, "lined up," or "possessors of rows."

'Aṭā' said: He means the rows of angels, and the people of each heaven are a separate row.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The people of each heaven, when they descend on the Day of Resurrection, will be a row encircling the earth and those upon it, so they will be seven rows.

﴿And Hell will be brought on that day﴾. "Yawma'idhin" is in the accusative governed by "jī'a." The one standing in place of the subject is "bi-Jahannam." Makkī permitted that "yawma'idhin" be the one standing in place of the subject, but that is not right.

Al-Wāḥidī said: A group of the exegetes said: It will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, bridled with seventy thousand bridles, with each bridle having seventy thousand angels dragging it, until it is placed on the left side of the Throne. No angel brought near, nor prophet sent, will remain without falling to his knees, saying: "O Lord, myself! myself!"

This which he transmitted from a group of exegetes will come, God willing, traced back to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

﴿On that day man will remember﴾. "Yawma'idhin" here is a substitute for the "yawma'idhin" preceding it, meaning: on the day Hell is brought, man will remember.

That is, he will take admonition, recall what he neglected, and regret what he sent ahead of himself in the world of disbelief and sins.

It was also said that the second "yawma'idhin" is a substitute for the phrase "idhā dukkat," and that the governing element for both is His words "yatadhakkaru al-insān."

﴿But how will the remembrance benefit him?﴾, meaning from where will he have remembrance and admonition? It was also said it is with an elided modifier: that is, from where will he have the benefit of the remembrance?

Al-Zajjāj said: He shows repentance, but from where is repentance?

﴿He will say, "Would that I had sent ahead for my life!"﴾ The sentence is a resumptive answer to an implied question, as if it was said: What will man say? It is also permissible that it is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) for His words "yatadhakkaru." The meaning: he wishes that he had sent ahead good and righteous deeds. The "lām" in "li-ḥayātī" means "for the sake of my life." What is meant is the life of the Hereafter, for it is the life in reality, because it is everlasting and not cut off.

It was also said that the "lām" means "in," and what is meant is the life of this world: that is, "Would that I had sent ahead righteous deeds during my life in the world, so that I might benefit from them this day." The first is preferable.

Al-Ḥasan said: By God, he knew that he had encountered a long life in which there is no death.

﴿So on that day none will punish as He punishes﴾, meaning on the day when the time of what has been mentioned of these conditions is, none will punish as God punishes. ﴿Nor will anyone bind as He binds﴾, or: none other than Him will undertake the punishment of God and His binding, since the whole matter belongs to Him. The two pronouns in both interpretations, in "'adhābihi" and "wathāqihi," refer to God, the Mighty and Majestic. This is according to the recitation of the majority, "yu'adhdhibu" and "yūthiqu," both in the active voice.

Al-Kisā'ī recited both in the passive voice, so the two pronouns refer back to man: that is, none will be punished with the punishment of that man, and none will be bound with his binding. "Al-insān" here means the disbeliever: that is, none who is not a disbeliever will be punished with the punishment of the disbeliever. It was also said it means Iblīs, and it was said it means Ubayy ibn Khalaf.

Al-Farrā' said: The meaning is that none will punish with the punishment of this specific disbeliever, nor bind with chains and shackles as he is bound, because of his extreme disbelief and obstinacy.

It was also said the meaning is: none will be punished in his place, and none will be bound in his place, so no ransom will be taken from him. This is like His words: ﴿And no bearer of burden shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'ām: 164]. "Al-'adhāb" is with the meaning of the punishing, and "al-wathāq" with the meaning of the binding.

Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred the recitation of al-Kisā'ī. He said: The pronoun in both places would be the pronoun of the disbeliever, since it is known that none punishes as God punishes.

Abū 'Alī al-Fārisī said: It is permissible that the pronoun refers to the disbeliever according to the recitation of the majority: that is, none punishes anyone as this disbeliever is punished.

When the Exalted finished relating the conditions of the wretched, He mentioned some conditions of the blessed, and so He said: ﴿O soul at peace﴾. "Al-muṭma'innah" is the one who is tranquil and certain in faith and in the oneness of God, who has reached the coolness of certainty (thalj al-yaqīn), such that no doubt mixes with it and no suspicion afflicts it.

Al-Ḥasan said: She is the believer who is certain.

Mujāhid said: She is the one content with God's decree, who knows that what missed her would never have been destined to reach her, and that what reached her would never have been destined to miss her.

Muqātil said: She is the safe and reassured one.

Ibn Kaysan said: "The tranquil soul" (al-mutma'innah) is the one at peace through the remembrance of God. It was also said: "the sincere one" (al-mukhlisah). Ibn Zayd said: it is called "the tranquil" because it was given the good news of Paradise at death and at the Resurrection.

﴿Return to your Lord﴾: that is, return to God, well-pleased with the reward He has given you, and well-pleasing in His sight. It was also said: return to His promise; and it was said: return to His command.

ʿIkrimah and ʿAta' said: the meaning of ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ is: return to your body in which you were. Ibn Jarir chose this view, and what supports it is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, "fa-odkhuli fi ʿabdi" (in the singular). The first view is preferable.

﴿Enter among My servants﴾: that is, among the company of My righteous servants; be one of them and join their ranks.

﴿And enter My Paradise﴾ along with them. It was said that she will be told "Return to your Lord" when she departs from this world, and she will be told "Enter among My servants and enter My Paradise" on the Day of Resurrection. The verse is meant in its general sense for every tranquil soul, and its revelation concerning a specific person does not preclude this; the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿eating (the inheritance) greedily (aklan lamma)﴾, that he said: "sweeping (safF)". And regarding His words ﴿love of wealth, immensely (hubban jamma)﴾, he said: "intensely." Ibn Jarir related from him also: ﴿aklan lamma﴾, he said: "intensely."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, regarding His words ﴿when the earth is leveled, leveled and leveled (dakkan dakka)﴾, that he said: "its shaking."

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "On that Day Hell will be brought forth, having seventy thousand bridles, with every bridle seventy thousand angels pulling it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿and how can he have the remembrance (wa-anna lahu al-dhikra)﴾ that he said: "And how could he?" Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His words ﴿on that Day none will punish as He punishes﴾ the verse, he said: "None will punish with the punishment of God, and none will bind with the bond of God."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from him also, regarding His words ﴿O tranquil soul﴾, he said: "the believing soul." ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ means: to your body.

He said: This verse was revealed while Abu Bakr was sitting, and he said: "O Messenger of God, how beautiful this is!" He said: "As for her, she will be told this."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nuʿaym in al-Hilyah related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr something similar, as a mursal report.

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul related something similar from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿O tranquil soul﴾ that it means "the one who affirms (the truth)."

Ibn Jarir related from him also regarding the verse that he said: "Souls will be returned to bodies on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding His words ﴿Return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ that he said: "with what she was given of reward, being well-pleased with her by her deeds." ﴿Enter among My servants﴾ means: the believers.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he said: Ibn ʿAbbas died at al-Ta'if, and a bird came, of a form not seen before, and entered his bier, and then it was not seen coming out of it. When he was buried, this verse was recited at the edge of the grave, and we do not know who recited it: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing, enter among My servants, and enter My Paradise.﴾

Abu Nuʿaym in al-Dala'il related something similar from ʿIkrimah.

Mujāhid said: He lap it up (yasiffuhu saffan).
