﴿And you love wealth with abundant love﴾, meaning intense love. "Al-jamm" is the abundant. It is said: "jamma al-mā' fī al-ḥawḍ," when the water increased and gathered. "Al-jamma" is the place where water gathers.

Then the Exalted repeated the deterrent and rebuke to them, and said: "Kallā," meaning this is not how your deeds should be.

Then the Exalted began anew, and said: ﴿When the earth is ground to powder, grinding upon grinding﴾. In this is a warning to them after the deterrent and rebuke. "Al-dakk" is breaking and crushing. The meaning here: it was shaken and moved with a movement after a movement.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Its mountains were crushed until they became level.

Al-Zajjāj said: That is, it was shaken and so some of it crushed others.

Al-Mubarrad said: That is, it was spread out and its elevation disappeared. He said: "al-dakk" is bringing down the elevated by flattening. The discussion of "al-dakk" has already preceded in the surah al-A'rāf and in the surah al-Aḥqāf. The meaning: it was crushed once after another. The accusative of the first "dakkan" is as a verbal noun emphasizing the verb, and the second "dakkan" is an emphasis of the first, so said Ibn 'Uṣfūr.

It is permissible that the accusative is as a circumstantial (ḥāl), meaning in the state of being crushed time after time, as one says: "I taught him arithmetic chapter by chapter (bāban bāban), and I taught him the script letter by letter (ḥarfan ḥarfan)." The meaning: He repeated the crushing upon it until it became scattered dust (habā'an munbaththan).

﴿And your Lord comes﴾, meaning His command and His decree comes, and His signs appear. It was also said the meaning is: the doubts on that day cease, and the realities become manifest and necessary, as doubt vanishes upon the arrival of the thing that was being doubted. It was also said: the subjugation of your Lord, His authority, and His sole control of the command and governance comes, without giving anyone of His servants any part of that. ﴿And the angels, rank upon rank﴾. The accusative of "ṣaffan ṣaffan" is as a circumstantial: that is, "lined up," or "possessors of rows."

'Aṭā' said: He means the rows of angels, and the people of each heaven are a separate row.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The people of each heaven, when they descend on the Day of Resurrection, will be a row encircling the earth and those upon it, so they will be seven rows.

﴿And Hell will be brought on that day﴾. "Yawma'idhin" is in the accusative governed by "jī'a." The one standing in place of the subject is "bi-Jahannam." Makkī permitted that "yawma'idhin" be the one standing in place of the subject, but that is not right.

Al-Wāḥidī said: A group of the exegetes said: It will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, bridled with seventy thousand bridles, with each bridle having seventy thousand angels dragging it, until it is placed on the left side of the Throne. No angel brought near, nor prophet sent, will remain without falling to his knees, saying: "O Lord, myself! myself!"

This which he transmitted from a group of exegetes will come, God willing, traced back to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

﴿On that day man will remember﴾. "Yawma'idhin" here is a substitute for the "yawma'idhin" preceding it, meaning: on the day Hell is brought, man will remember.

That is, he will take admonition, recall what he neglected, and regret what he sent ahead of himself in the world of disbelief and sins.

It was also said that the second "yawma'idhin" is a substitute for the phrase "idhā dukkat," and that the governing element for both is His words "yatadhakkaru al-insān."

﴿But how will the remembrance benefit him?﴾, meaning from where will he have remembrance and admonition? It was also said it is with an elided modifier: that is, from where will he have the benefit of the remembrance?

Al-Zajjāj said: He shows repentance, but from where is repentance?

﴿He will say, "Would that I had sent ahead for my life!"﴾ The sentence is a resumptive answer to an implied question, as if it was said: What will man say? It is also permissible that it is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) for His words "yatadhakkaru." The meaning: he wishes that he had sent ahead good and righteous deeds. The "lām" in "li-ḥayātī" means "for the sake of my life." What is meant is the life of the Hereafter, for it is the life in reality, because it is everlasting and not cut off.

It was also said that the "lām" means "in," and what is meant is the life of this world: that is, "Would that I had sent ahead righteous deeds during my life in the world, so that I might benefit from them this day." The first is preferable.

Al-Ḥasan said: By God, he knew that he had encountered a long life in which there is no death.

﴿So on that day none will punish as He punishes﴾, meaning on the day when the time of what has been mentioned of these conditions is, none will punish as God punishes. ﴿Nor will anyone bind as He binds﴾, or: none other than Him will undertake the punishment of God and His binding, since the whole matter belongs to Him. The two pronouns in both interpretations, in "'adhābihi" and "wathāqihi," refer to God, the Mighty and Majestic. This is according to the recitation of the majority, "yu'adhdhibu" and "yūthiqu," both in the active voice.

Al-Kisā'ī recited both in the passive voice, so the two pronouns refer back to man: that is, none will be punished with the punishment of that man, and none will be bound with his binding. "Al-insān" here means the disbeliever: that is, none who is not a disbeliever will be punished with the punishment of the disbeliever. It was also said it means Iblīs, and it was said it means Ubayy ibn Khalaf.

Al-Farrā' said: The meaning is that none will punish with the punishment of this specific disbeliever, nor bind with chains and shackles as he is bound, because of his extreme disbelief and obstinacy.

It was also said the meaning is: none will be punished in his place, and none will be bound in his place, so no ransom will be taken from him. This is like His words: ﴿And no bearer of burden shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'ām: 164]. "Al-'adhāb" is with the meaning of the punishing, and "al-wathāq" with the meaning of the binding.

Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred the recitation of al-Kisā'ī. He said: The pronoun in both places would be the pronoun of the disbeliever, since it is known that none punishes as God punishes.

Abū 'Alī al-Fārisī said: It is permissible that the pronoun refers to the disbeliever according to the recitation of the majority: that is, none punishes anyone as this disbeliever is punished.

When the Exalted finished relating the conditions of the wretched, He mentioned some conditions of the blessed, and so He said: ﴿O soul at peace﴾. "Al-muṭma'innah" is the one who is tranquil and certain in faith and in the oneness of God, who has reached the coolness of certainty (thalj al-yaqīn), such that no doubt mixes with it and no suspicion afflicts it.

Al-Ḥasan said: She is the believer who is certain.

Mujāhid said: She is the one content with God's decree, who knows that what missed her would never have been destined to reach her, and that what reached her would never have been destined to miss her.

Muqātil said: She is the safe and reassured one.

Ibn Kaysan said: "The tranquil soul" (al-mutma'innah) is the one at peace through the remembrance of God. It was also said: "the sincere one" (al-mukhlisah). Ibn Zayd said: it is called "the tranquil" because it was given the good news of Paradise at death and at the Resurrection.

﴿Return to your Lord﴾: that is, return to God, well-pleased with the reward He has given you, and well-pleasing in His sight. It was also said: return to His promise; and it was said: return to His command.

ʿIkrimah and ʿAta' said: the meaning of ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ is: return to your body in which you were. Ibn Jarir chose this view, and what supports it is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, "fa-odkhuli fi ʿabdi" (in the singular). The first view is preferable.

﴿Enter among My servants﴾: that is, among the company of My righteous servants; be one of them and join their ranks.

﴿And enter My Paradise﴾ along with them. It was said that she will be told "Return to your Lord" when she departs from this world, and she will be told "Enter among My servants and enter My Paradise" on the Day of Resurrection. The verse is meant in its general sense for every tranquil soul, and its revelation concerning a specific person does not preclude this; the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿eating (the inheritance) greedily (aklan lamma)﴾, that he said: "sweeping (safF)". And regarding His words ﴿love of wealth, immensely (hubban jamma)﴾, he said: "intensely." Ibn Jarir related from him also: ﴿aklan lamma﴾, he said: "intensely."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, regarding His words ﴿when the earth is leveled, leveled and leveled (dakkan dakka)﴾, that he said: "its shaking."

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "On that Day Hell will be brought forth, having seventy thousand bridles, with every bridle seventy thousand angels pulling it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿and how can he have the remembrance (wa-anna lahu al-dhikra)﴾ that he said: "And how could he?" Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His words ﴿on that Day none will punish as He punishes﴾ the verse, he said: "None will punish with the punishment of God, and none will bind with the bond of God."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from him also, regarding His words ﴿O tranquil soul﴾, he said: "the believing soul." ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ means: to your body.

He said: This verse was revealed while Abu Bakr was sitting, and he said: "O Messenger of God, how beautiful this is!" He said: "As for her, she will be told this."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nuʿaym in al-Hilyah related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr something similar, as a mursal report.

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul related something similar from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿O tranquil soul﴾ that it means "the one who affirms (the truth)."

Ibn Jarir related from him also regarding the verse that he said: "Souls will be returned to bodies on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding His words ﴿Return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ that he said: "with what she was given of reward, being well-pleased with her by her deeds." ﴿Enter among My servants﴾ means: the believers.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he said: Ibn ʿAbbas died at al-Ta'if, and a bird came, of a form not seen before, and entered his bier, and then it was not seen coming out of it. When he was buried, this verse was recited at the edge of the grave, and we do not know who recited it: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing, enter among My servants, and enter My Paradise.﴾

Abu Nuʿaym in al-Dala'il related something similar from ʿIkrimah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 89, verses 15–30 (part 1 of 2):

When the Exalted mentioned that He is ever watchful (bi-l-mirsad), He mentioned what indicates the variation in His servants' conditions upon receiving good and upon receiving evil, and that the object of their gaze and the greatest of their aims is this world. So He said: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him﴾, meaning He tries and examines him with blessings, ﴿and honors him and bestows favor upon him﴾, meaning He honors him with wealth and widens his provision. ﴿Then he says, "My Lord has honored me,"﴾ rejoicing in what he has attained and delighted in what he has been given, not thankful to God for it, and not considering that this is a trial from his Lord, a test of his state and a disclosure of what he harbors of patience, impatience, gratitude for the blessing, or ingratitude for it. The "mā" in His words "idhā mā" is superfluous (zā'idah). His words ﴿and honors him and bestows favor upon him﴾ are an explanation of the "testing." The meaning of "akramanī" is: He has favored me with the wealth He has given me and lavished blessings upon me, because I deserve it more and because I am its appropriate recipient. "Al-insān" is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "fa-yaqūlu rabbī akramanī." The "fa" entered into it because "amma" (as for) carries the sense of a conditional. The adverbial phrase placed between the subject and the predicate, although it precedes in wording, is delayed in meaning. That is: "As for man, then he says, 'My Lord has honored me,' at the time of his being tested with favors."

Al-Kalbi said: "al-Insān" is the disbeliever, Ubayy ibn Khalaf.

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Umayya ibn Khalaf. It was also said it was revealed concerning Utba ibn Rabi'a and Abu Hudhayfa ibn al-Mughira.

﴿But as for when He tests him﴾, meaning He examines him and treats him as one who is being examined, ﴿and so restricts his provision for him﴾, meaning He constricts it and does not widen it for him nor extends it to him. ﴿Then he says, "My Lord has humiliated me,"﴾ meaning He has assigned him humiliation. This is the attribute of the disbeliever who does not believe in the Resurrection, for to him there is no honor except the world and the widening of its enjoyments, and there is no humiliation to him except losing them and failing to reach what he desires of its adornments. As for the believer, honor for him is that God honors him by his obedience and enables him to perform the works of the Hereafter. It is possible that "al-insān" is intended in a general sense, because of his lack of certainty that what came to him of good in this world and what befell him of evil are nothing but a test and an examination, and that the whole world is not worth, in the sight of God, the wing of a mosquito. Had it been worth the wing of a mosquito, He would not have given the disbeliever a single sip of water from it.

Nāfi' recited with the ya' (the final long vowel) affirmed in "akramanī" and "ahānanī" when connected, and omitted them when pausing. Ibn Kathīr, in the transmission of al-Bazzī from him, and Ibn Muḥaysin, and Ya'qūb recited with both affirmed, both in connection and in pause. The rest recited with both omitted in connection and in pause, following the orthography of the Muṣḥaf (the written codex) and for conformity with the ends of verses (ru'ūs al-āy). The original form is with them affirmed, since it is a noun (ism). Among the omission is the poet's verse:

"And from an enemy whose hidden rancor is apparent, when I stand before him, he disowned me (ankaranī)."

That is, "ankaranī" (he disowned me).

Al-Jumhūr recited "fa-qadara" with the light form (takhfīf), and Ibn 'Āmir recited it with the doubled form (tashdīd), and both are dialects.

Al-Ḥaramayn (Ibn Kathīr and Nāfi') and Abū 'Amr recited "rabbī" with a fatḥa on the ya' in both places, and the rest recited it with sukūn.

His words "kallā" (no indeed) are a deterrent to man who said what he said in both states, and a rebuke to him. For God, the Exalted, may widen provision and extend blessings to a person, not as a sign of his honor, and He may constrict it for him, not as a sign of his humiliation, but for testing and examination, as has preceded.

Al-Farrā' said: "Kallā" in this place means: it was not fitting for the servant to be in this condition, but rather he should praise God for wealth and for poverty.

Then the Exalted moved from describing the evil of man's words to describing the evil of his deeds, and so He said: ﴿Nay, you do not honor the orphan﴾. The turn to direct address (al-iltifāt ilā al-khiṭāb) is for the purpose of reproach and censure, according to the recitation of the majority with the second-person form (al-fawqiyyah).

Al-Jumhūr recited "taḥāḍḍūna," "ta'kulūna," and "tuḥibbūna" with the second-person form (al-fawqiyyah) for address in them.

Abū 'Amr and Ya'qūb recited them with the third-person form (al-taḥtiyyah). The plural in these verbs is in view of the meaning of "al-insān," because what is meant by it is the category. That is: "Nay, you have deeds that are uglier than what has been mentioned, namely that you abandon honoring the orphan, so you eat his wealth and withhold from him the surplus of your own wealth."

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Qudāma ibn Maẓ'ūn, who was an orphan in the custody of Umayya ibn Khalaf.

﴿And you do not urge one another to feed the needy﴾. Al-Jumhūr recited "tuḥḍḍūna," from "ḥaddahu 'alā kadhā," meaning he incited him to it, and its object is omitted: that is, "you do not urge yourselves," or "none of you urges another to that, nor commands it, nor guides to it." The Kufans recited "tataḥāḍḍūna" with a fatḥa on the tā' and an alif after the ḥā', and its origin is "tataḥāḍḍūna," so one of the two tā's is dropped: that is, "none of you urges another."

Al-Kisā'ī in one of the transmissions from him, and al-Sulamī, recited "tuḥāḍḍūna" with a ḍamma on the tā', from al-ḥaḍḍ, which is urging. His words ﴿on the feeding of the needy﴾ are related to "tuḥḍḍūna." It is either a verbal noun (ism maṣdar), meaning "on feeding the needy," or a noun for the food, and it would then be with an elided modifier (ḥadhf muḍāf), meaning "on giving out the food of the needy," or "on giving the food of the needy."

﴿And you devour the inheritance﴾. Its origin is "al-wurāth," so the tā' was substituted for a ḍammed wāw, as in "tujāh" and "wijāh." What is meant by it is the wealth of orphans who inherit it from their relatives, and likewise the wealth of women. That is because they used not to give inheritance to women and children, and they would consume their wealth ﴿with greedy devouring﴾, meaning intense devouring. It was also said the meaning of "lamman" is gathering, from the saying: "lamamtu al-ṭa'ām," when you ate all of it.

Al-Ḥasan said: He eats his own share and the share of the orphan. Abū 'Ubayda said likewise.

The original meaning of "al-lamm" in Arabic speech is gathering. It is said: "lamamtu al-shay' alummuhu lamman," meaning I gathered it. From this is the saying: "lamma Allāh sha'athahu," meaning God gathered what had scattered of his affairs. From this is the verse of al-Nābigha:

"You are not one who would leave behind a brother whom you do not gather up, despite his disorder; which of men is refined?"

Al-Layth said: "al-lamm" is intense gathering, and from it come "ḥajar malmūm" (a gathered stone) and "katība malmūma" (a gathered army). The one who eats "yalummu al-tharīd," meaning he gathers the bread-and-broth and then eats it.

Mujāhid said: He lap it up (yasiffuhu saffan).

Ibn Zayd said: When he has consumed his own wealth, he gathers together the wealth of others and eats it, without considering what he has eaten of the foul and the good.

﴿And you love wealth with abundant love﴾, meaning intense love. "Al-jamm" is the abundant. It is said: "jamma al-mā' fī al-ḥawḍ," when the water increased and gathered. "Al-jamma" is the place where water gathers.

Then the Exalted repeated the deterrent and rebuke to them, and said: "Kallā," meaning this is not how your deeds should be.

Then the Exalted began anew, and said: ﴿When the earth is ground to powder, grinding upon grinding﴾. In this is a warning to them after the deterrent and rebuke. "Al-dakk" is breaking and crushing. The meaning here: it was shaken and moved with a movement after a movement.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Its mountains were crushed until they became level.

Al-Zajjāj said: That is, it was shaken and so some of it crushed others.

Al-Mubarrad said: That is, it was spread out and its elevation disappeared. He said: "al-dakk" is bringing down the elevated by flattening. The discussion of "al-dakk" has already preceded in the surah al-A'rāf and in the surah al-Aḥqāf. The meaning: it was crushed once after another. The accusative of the first "dakkan" is as a verbal noun emphasizing the verb, and the second "dakkan" is an emphasis of the first, so said Ibn 'Uṣfūr.

It is permissible that the accusative is as a circumstantial (ḥāl), meaning in the state of being crushed time after time, as one says: "I taught him arithmetic chapter by chapter (bāban bāban), and I taught him the script letter by letter (ḥarfan ḥarfan)." The meaning: He repeated the crushing upon it until it became scattered dust (habā'an munbaththan).

﴿And your Lord comes﴾, meaning His command and His decree comes, and His signs appear. It was also said the meaning is: the doubts on that day cease, and the realities become manifest and necessary, as doubt vanishes upon the arrival of the thing that was being doubted. It was also said: the subjugation of your Lord, His authority, and His sole control of the command and governance comes, without giving anyone of His servants any part of that. ﴿And the angels, rank upon rank﴾. The accusative of "ṣaffan ṣaffan" is as a circumstantial: that is, "lined up," or "possessors of rows."

'Aṭā' said: He means the rows of angels, and the people of each heaven are a separate row.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The people of each heaven, when they descend on the Day of Resurrection, will be a row encircling the earth and those upon it, so they will be seven rows.

﴿And Hell will be brought on that day﴾. "Yawma'idhin" is in the accusative governed by "jī'a." The one standing in place of the subject is "bi-Jahannam." Makkī permitted that "yawma'idhin" be the one standing in place of the subject, but that is not right.

Al-Wāḥidī said: A group of the exegetes said: It will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, bridled with seventy thousand bridles, with each bridle having seventy thousand angels dragging it, until it is placed on the left side of the Throne. No angel brought near, nor prophet sent, will remain without falling to his knees, saying: "O Lord, myself! myself!"

This which he transmitted from a group of exegetes will come, God willing, traced back to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

﴿On that day man will remember﴾. "Yawma'idhin" here is a substitute for the "yawma'idhin" preceding it, meaning: on the day Hell is brought, man will remember.

That is, he will take admonition, recall what he neglected, and regret what he sent ahead of himself in the world of disbelief and sins.

It was also said that the second "yawma'idhin" is a substitute for the phrase "idhā dukkat," and that the governing element for both is His words "yatadhakkaru al-insān."

﴿But how will the remembrance benefit him?﴾, meaning from where will he have remembrance and admonition? It was also said it is with an elided modifier: that is, from where will he have the benefit of the remembrance?

Al-Zajjāj said: He shows repentance, but from where is repentance?

﴿He will say, "Would that I had sent ahead for my life!"﴾ The sentence is a resumptive answer to an implied question, as if it was said: What will man say? It is also permissible that it is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) for His words "yatadhakkaru." The meaning: he wishes that he had sent ahead good and righteous deeds. The "lām" in "li-ḥayātī" means "for the sake of my life." What is meant is the life of the Hereafter, for it is the life in reality, because it is everlasting and not cut off.

It was also said that the "lām" means "in," and what is meant is the life of this world: that is, "Would that I had sent ahead righteous deeds during my life in the world, so that I might benefit from them this day." The first is preferable.

Al-Ḥasan said: By God, he knew that he had encountered a long life in which there is no death.

﴿So on that day none will punish as He punishes﴾, meaning on the day when the time of what has been mentioned of these conditions is, none will punish as God punishes. ﴿Nor will anyone bind as He binds﴾, or: none other than Him will undertake the punishment of God and His binding, since the whole matter belongs to Him. The two pronouns in both interpretations, in "'adhābihi" and "wathāqihi," refer to God, the Mighty and Majestic. This is according to the recitation of the majority, "yu'adhdhibu" and "yūthiqu," both in the active voice.

Al-Kisā'ī recited both in the passive voice, so the two pronouns refer back to man: that is, none will be punished with the punishment of that man, and none will be bound with his binding. "Al-insān" here means the disbeliever: that is, none who is not a disbeliever will be punished with the punishment of the disbeliever. It was also said it means Iblīs, and it was said it means Ubayy ibn Khalaf.

Al-Farrā' said: The meaning is that none will punish with the punishment of this specific disbeliever, nor bind with chains and shackles as he is bound, because of his extreme disbelief and obstinacy.

It was also said the meaning is: none will be punished in his place, and none will be bound in his place, so no ransom will be taken from him. This is like His words: ﴿And no bearer of burden shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'ām: 164]. "Al-'adhāb" is with the meaning of the punishing, and "al-wathāq" with the meaning of the binding.

Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred the recitation of al-Kisā'ī. He said: The pronoun in both places would be the pronoun of the disbeliever, since it is known that none punishes as God punishes.

Abū 'Alī al-Fārisī said: It is permissible that the pronoun refers to the disbeliever according to the recitation of the majority: that is, none punishes anyone as this disbeliever is punished.

When the Exalted finished relating the conditions of the wretched, He mentioned some conditions of the blessed, and so He said: ﴿O soul at peace﴾. "Al-muṭma'innah" is the one who is tranquil and certain in faith and in the oneness of God, who has reached the coolness of certainty (thalj al-yaqīn), such that no doubt mixes with it and no suspicion afflicts it.

Al-Ḥasan said: She is the believer who is certain.

Mujāhid said: She is the one content with God's decree, who knows that what missed her would never have been destined to reach her, and that what reached her would never have been destined to miss her.

Muqātil said: She is the safe and reassured one.

Ibn Kaysan said: "The tranquil soul" (al-mutma'innah) is the one at peace through the remembrance of God. It was also said: "the sincere one" (al-mukhlisah). Ibn Zayd said: it is called "the tranquil" because it was given the good news of Paradise at death and at the Resurrection.

﴿Return to your Lord﴾: that is, return to God, well-pleased with the reward He has given you, and well-pleasing in His sight. It was also said: return to His promise; and it was said: return to His command.

ʿIkrimah and ʿAta' said: the meaning of ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ is: return to your body in which you were. Ibn Jarir chose this view, and what supports it is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, "fa-odkhuli fi ʿabdi" (in the singular). The first view is preferable.

﴿Enter among My servants﴾: that is, among the company of My righteous servants; be one of them and join their ranks.

﴿And enter My Paradise﴾ along with them. It was said that she will be told "Return to your Lord" when she departs from this world, and she will be told "Enter among My servants and enter My Paradise" on the Day of Resurrection. The verse is meant in its general sense for every tranquil soul, and its revelation concerning a specific person does not preclude this; the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿eating (the inheritance) greedily (aklan lamma)﴾, that he said: "sweeping (safF)". And regarding His words ﴿love of wealth, immensely (hubban jamma)﴾, he said: "intensely." Ibn Jarir related from him also: ﴿aklan lamma﴾, he said: "intensely."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, regarding His words ﴿when the earth is leveled, leveled and leveled (dakkan dakka)﴾, that he said: "its shaking."

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "On that Day Hell will be brought forth, having seventy thousand bridles, with every bridle seventy thousand angels pulling it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿and how can he have the remembrance (wa-anna lahu al-dhikra)﴾ that he said: "And how could he?" Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His words ﴿on that Day none will punish as He punishes﴾ the verse, he said: "None will punish with the punishment of God, and none will bind with the bond of God."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from him also, regarding His words ﴿O tranquil soul﴾, he said: "the believing soul." ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ means: to your body.

He said: This verse was revealed while Abu Bakr was sitting, and he said: "O Messenger of God, how beautiful this is!" He said: "As for her, she will be told this."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nuʿaym in al-Hilyah related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr something similar, as a mursal report.

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul related something similar from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

Ibn Jarir related from him also regarding the verse that he said: "Souls will be returned to bodies on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding His words ﴿Return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ that he said: "with what she was given of reward, being well-pleased with her by her deeds." ﴿Enter among My servants﴾ means: the believers.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he said: Ibn ʿAbbas died at al-Ta'if, and a bird came, of a form not seen before, and entered his bier, and then it was not seen coming out of it. When he was buried, this verse was recited at the edge of the grave, and we do not know who recited it: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing, enter among My servants, and enter My Paradise.﴾

Abu Nuʿaym in al-Dala'il related something similar from ʿIkrimah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 89, verses 15–30 (part 1 of 2):

When the Exalted mentioned that He is ever watchful (bi-l-mirsad), He mentioned what indicates the variation in His servants' conditions upon receiving good and upon receiving evil, and that the object of their gaze and the greatest of their aims is this world. So He said: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him﴾, meaning He tries and examines him with blessings, ﴿and honors him and bestows favor upon him﴾, meaning He honors him with wealth and widens his provision. ﴿Then he says, "My Lord has honored me,"﴾ rejoicing in what he has attained and delighted in what he has been given, not thankful to God for it, and not considering that this is a trial from his Lord, a test of his state and a disclosure of what he harbors of patience, impatience, gratitude for the blessing, or ingratitude for it. The "mā" in His words "idhā mā" is superfluous (zā'idah). His words ﴿and honors him and bestows favor upon him﴾ are an explanation of the "testing." The meaning of "akramanī" is: He has favored me with the wealth He has given me and lavished blessings upon me, because I deserve it more and because I am its appropriate recipient. "Al-insān" is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "fa-yaqūlu rabbī akramanī." The "fa" entered into it because "amma" (as for) carries the sense of a conditional. The adverbial phrase placed between the subject and the predicate, although it precedes in wording, is delayed in meaning. That is: "As for man, then he says, 'My Lord has honored me,' at the time of his being tested with favors."

Al-Kalbi said: "al-Insān" is the disbeliever, Ubayy ibn Khalaf.

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Umayya ibn Khalaf. It was also said it was revealed concerning Utba ibn Rabi'a and Abu Hudhayfa ibn al-Mughira.

﴿But as for when He tests him﴾, meaning He examines him and treats him as one who is being examined, ﴿and so restricts his provision for him﴾, meaning He constricts it and does not widen it for him nor extends it to him. ﴿Then he says, "My Lord has humiliated me,"﴾ meaning He has assigned him humiliation. This is the attribute of the disbeliever who does not believe in the Resurrection, for to him there is no honor except the world and the widening of its enjoyments, and there is no humiliation to him except losing them and failing to reach what he desires of its adornments. As for the believer, honor for him is that God honors him by his obedience and enables him to perform the works of the Hereafter. It is possible that "al-insān" is intended in a general sense, because of his lack of certainty that what came to him of good in this world and what befell him of evil are nothing but a test and an examination, and that the whole world is not worth, in the sight of God, the wing of a mosquito. Had it been worth the wing of a mosquito, He would not have given the disbeliever a single sip of water from it.

Nāfi' recited with the ya' (the final long vowel) affirmed in "akramanī" and "ahānanī" when connected, and omitted them when pausing. Ibn Kathīr, in the transmission of al-Bazzī from him, and Ibn Muḥaysin, and Ya'qūb recited with both affirmed, both in connection and in pause. The rest recited with both omitted in connection and in pause, following the orthography of the Muṣḥaf (the written codex) and for conformity with the ends of verses (ru'ūs al-āy). The original form is with them affirmed, since it is a noun (ism). Among the omission is the poet's verse:

"And from an enemy whose hidden rancor is apparent, when I stand before him, he disowned me (ankaranī)."

That is, "ankaranī" (he disowned me).

Al-Jumhūr recited "fa-qadara" with the light form (takhfīf), and Ibn 'Āmir recited it with the doubled form (tashdīd), and both are dialects.

Al-Ḥaramayn (Ibn Kathīr and Nāfi') and Abū 'Amr recited "rabbī" with a fatḥa on the ya' in both places, and the rest recited it with sukūn.

His words "kallā" (no indeed) are a deterrent to man who said what he said in both states, and a rebuke to him. For God, the Exalted, may widen provision and extend blessings to a person, not as a sign of his honor, and He may constrict it for him, not as a sign of his humiliation, but for testing and examination, as has preceded.

Al-Farrā' said: "Kallā" in this place means: it was not fitting for the servant to be in this condition, but rather he should praise God for wealth and for poverty.

Then the Exalted moved from describing the evil of man's words to describing the evil of his deeds, and so He said: ﴿Nay, you do not honor the orphan﴾. The turn to direct address (al-iltifāt ilā al-khiṭāb) is for the purpose of reproach and censure, according to the recitation of the majority with the second-person form (al-fawqiyyah).

Al-Jumhūr recited "taḥāḍḍūna," "ta'kulūna," and "tuḥibbūna" with the second-person form (al-fawqiyyah) for address in them.

Abū 'Amr and Ya'qūb recited them with the third-person form (al-taḥtiyyah). The plural in these verbs is in view of the meaning of "al-insān," because what is meant by it is the category. That is: "Nay, you have deeds that are uglier than what has been mentioned, namely that you abandon honoring the orphan, so you eat his wealth and withhold from him the surplus of your own wealth."

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Qudāma ibn Maẓ'ūn, who was an orphan in the custody of Umayya ibn Khalaf.

﴿And you do not urge one another to feed the needy﴾. Al-Jumhūr recited "tuḥḍḍūna," from "ḥaddahu 'alā kadhā," meaning he incited him to it, and its object is omitted: that is, "you do not urge yourselves," or "none of you urges another to that, nor commands it, nor guides to it." The Kufans recited "tataḥāḍḍūna" with a fatḥa on the tā' and an alif after the ḥā', and its origin is "tataḥāḍḍūna," so one of the two tā's is dropped: that is, "none of you urges another."

Al-Kisā'ī in one of the transmissions from him, and al-Sulamī, recited "tuḥāḍḍūna" with a ḍamma on the tā', from al-ḥaḍḍ, which is urging. His words ﴿on the feeding of the needy﴾ are related to "tuḥḍḍūna." It is either a verbal noun (ism maṣdar), meaning "on feeding the needy," or a noun for the food, and it would then be with an elided modifier (ḥadhf muḍāf), meaning "on giving out the food of the needy," or "on giving the food of the needy."

﴿And you devour the inheritance﴾. Its origin is "al-wurāth," so the tā' was substituted for a ḍammed wāw, as in "tujāh" and "wijāh." What is meant by it is the wealth of orphans who inherit it from their relatives, and likewise the wealth of women. That is because they used not to give inheritance to women and children, and they would consume their wealth ﴿with greedy devouring﴾, meaning intense devouring. It was also said the meaning of "lamman" is gathering, from the saying: "lamamtu al-ṭa'ām," when you ate all of it.

Al-Ḥasan said: He eats his own share and the share of the orphan. Abū 'Ubayda said likewise.

The original meaning of "al-lamm" in Arabic speech is gathering. It is said: "lamamtu al-shay' alummuhu lamman," meaning I gathered it. From this is the saying: "lamma Allāh sha'athahu," meaning God gathered what had scattered of his affairs. From this is the verse of al-Nābigha:

"You are not one who would leave behind a brother whom you do not gather up, despite his disorder; which of men is refined?"

Al-Layth said: "al-lamm" is intense gathering, and from it come "ḥajar malmūm" (a gathered stone) and "katība malmūma" (a gathered army). The one who eats "yalummu al-tharīd," meaning he gathers the bread-and-broth and then eats it.

Mujāhid said: He lap it up (yasiffuhu saffan).

Ibn Zayd said: When he has consumed his own wealth, he gathers together the wealth of others and eats it, without considering what he has eaten of the foul and the good.

﴿And you love wealth with abundant love﴾, meaning intense love. "Al-jamm" is the abundant. It is said: "jamma al-mā' fī al-ḥawḍ," when the water increased and gathered. "Al-jamma" is the place where water gathers.

Then the Exalted repeated the deterrent and rebuke to them, and said: "Kallā," meaning this is not how your deeds should be.

Then the Exalted began anew, and said: ﴿When the earth is ground to powder, grinding upon grinding﴾. In this is a warning to them after the deterrent and rebuke. "Al-dakk" is breaking and crushing. The meaning here: it was shaken and moved with a movement after a movement.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Its mountains were crushed until they became level.

Al-Zajjāj said: That is, it was shaken and so some of it crushed others.

Al-Mubarrad said: That is, it was spread out and its elevation disappeared. He said: "al-dakk" is bringing down the elevated by flattening. The discussion of "al-dakk" has already preceded in the surah al-A'rāf and in the surah al-Aḥqāf. The meaning: it was crushed once after another. The accusative of the first "dakkan" is as a verbal noun emphasizing the verb, and the second "dakkan" is an emphasis of the first, so said Ibn 'Uṣfūr.

It is permissible that the accusative is as a circumstantial (ḥāl), meaning in the state of being crushed time after time, as one says: "I taught him arithmetic chapter by chapter (bāban bāban), and I taught him the script letter by letter (ḥarfan ḥarfan)." The meaning: He repeated the crushing upon it until it became scattered dust (habā'an munbaththan).

﴿And your Lord comes﴾, meaning His command and His decree comes, and His signs appear. It was also said the meaning is: the doubts on that day cease, and the realities become manifest and necessary, as doubt vanishes upon the arrival of the thing that was being doubted. It was also said: the subjugation of your Lord, His authority, and His sole control of the command and governance comes, without giving anyone of His servants any part of that. ﴿And the angels, rank upon rank﴾. The accusative of "ṣaffan ṣaffan" is as a circumstantial: that is, "lined up," or "possessors of rows."

'Aṭā' said: He means the rows of angels, and the people of each heaven are a separate row.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The people of each heaven, when they descend on the Day of Resurrection, will be a row encircling the earth and those upon it, so they will be seven rows.

﴿And Hell will be brought on that day﴾. "Yawma'idhin" is in the accusative governed by "jī'a." The one standing in place of the subject is "bi-Jahannam." Makkī permitted that "yawma'idhin" be the one standing in place of the subject, but that is not right.

Al-Wāḥidī said: A group of the exegetes said: It will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, bridled with seventy thousand bridles, with each bridle having seventy thousand angels dragging it, until it is placed on the left side of the Throne. No angel brought near, nor prophet sent, will remain without falling to his knees, saying: "O Lord, myself! myself!"

This which he transmitted from a group of exegetes will come, God willing, traced back to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

﴿On that day man will remember﴾. "Yawma'idhin" here is a substitute for the "yawma'idhin" preceding it, meaning: on the day Hell is brought, man will remember.

That is, he will take admonition, recall what he neglected, and regret what he sent ahead of himself in the world of disbelief and sins.

It was also said that the second "yawma'idhin" is a substitute for the phrase "idhā dukkat," and that the governing element for both is His words "yatadhakkaru al-insān."

﴿But how will the remembrance benefit him?﴾, meaning from where will he have remembrance and admonition? It was also said it is with an elided modifier: that is, from where will he have the benefit of the remembrance?

Al-Zajjāj said: He shows repentance, but from where is repentance?

﴿He will say, "Would that I had sent ahead for my life!"﴾ The sentence is a resumptive answer to an implied question, as if it was said: What will man say? It is also permissible that it is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) for His words "yatadhakkaru." The meaning: he wishes that he had sent ahead good and righteous deeds. The "lām" in "li-ḥayātī" means "for the sake of my life." What is meant is the life of the Hereafter, for it is the life in reality, because it is everlasting and not cut off.

It was also said that the "lām" means "in," and what is meant is the life of this world: that is, "Would that I had sent ahead righteous deeds during my life in the world, so that I might benefit from them this day." The first is preferable.

Al-Ḥasan said: By God, he knew that he had encountered a long life in which there is no death.

﴿So on that day none will punish as He punishes﴾, meaning on the day when the time of what has been mentioned of these conditions is, none will punish as God punishes. ﴿Nor will anyone bind as He binds﴾, or: none other than Him will undertake the punishment of God and His binding, since the whole matter belongs to Him. The two pronouns in both interpretations, in "'adhābihi" and "wathāqihi," refer to God, the Mighty and Majestic. This is according to the recitation of the majority, "yu'adhdhibu" and "yūthiqu," both in the active voice.

Al-Kisā'ī recited both in the passive voice, so the two pronouns refer back to man: that is, none will be punished with the punishment of that man, and none will be bound with his binding. "Al-insān" here means the disbeliever: that is, none who is not a disbeliever will be punished with the punishment of the disbeliever. It was also said it means Iblīs, and it was said it means Ubayy ibn Khalaf.

Al-Farrā' said: The meaning is that none will punish with the punishment of this specific disbeliever, nor bind with chains and shackles as he is bound, because of his extreme disbelief and obstinacy.

It was also said the meaning is: none will be punished in his place, and none will be bound in his place, so no ransom will be taken from him. This is like His words: ﴿And no bearer of burden shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'ām: 164]. "Al-'adhāb" is with the meaning of the punishing, and "al-wathāq" with the meaning of the binding.

Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred the recitation of al-Kisā'ī. He said: The pronoun in both places would be the pronoun of the disbeliever, since it is known that none punishes as God punishes.

Abū 'Alī al-Fārisī said: It is permissible that the pronoun refers to the disbeliever according to the recitation of the majority: that is, none punishes anyone as this disbeliever is punished.

When the Exalted finished relating the conditions of the wretched, He mentioned some conditions of the blessed, and so He said: ﴿O soul at peace﴾. "Al-muṭma'innah" is the one who is tranquil and certain in faith and in the oneness of God, who has reached the coolness of certainty (thalj al-yaqīn), such that no doubt mixes with it and no suspicion afflicts it.

Al-Ḥasan said: She is the believer who is certain.

Mujāhid said: She is the one content with God's decree, who knows that what missed her would never have been destined to reach her, and that what reached her would never have been destined to miss her.

Muqātil said: She is the safe and reassured one.

Ibn Kaysan said: "The tranquil soul" (al-mutma'innah) is the one at peace through the remembrance of God. It was also said: "the sincere one" (al-mukhlisah). Ibn Zayd said: it is called "the tranquil" because it was given the good news of Paradise at death and at the Resurrection.

﴿Return to your Lord﴾: that is, return to God, well-pleased with the reward He has given you, and well-pleasing in His sight. It was also said: return to His promise; and it was said: return to His command.

ʿIkrimah and ʿAta' said: the meaning of ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ is: return to your body in which you were. Ibn Jarir chose this view, and what supports it is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, "fa-odkhuli fi ʿabdi" (in the singular). The first view is preferable.

﴿Enter among My servants﴾: that is, among the company of My righteous servants; be one of them and join their ranks.

﴿And enter My Paradise﴾ along with them. It was said that she will be told "Return to your Lord" when she departs from this world, and she will be told "Enter among My servants and enter My Paradise" on the Day of Resurrection. The verse is meant in its general sense for every tranquil soul, and its revelation concerning a specific person does not preclude this; the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿eating (the inheritance) greedily (aklan lamma)﴾, that he said: "sweeping (safF)". And regarding His words ﴿love of wealth, immensely (hubban jamma)﴾, he said: "intensely." Ibn Jarir related from him also: ﴿aklan lamma﴾, he said: "intensely."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿and how can he have the remembrance (wa-anna lahu al-dhikra)﴾ that he said: "And how could he?" al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul related something similar from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

Ibn Jarir related from him also regarding the verse that he said: "Souls will be returned to bodies on the Day of Resurrection."

His words "kallā" (no indeed) are a deterrent to man who said what he said in both states, and a rebuke to him. For God, the Exalted, may widen provision and extend blessings to a person, not as a sign of his honor, and He may constrict it for him, not as a sign of his humiliation, but for testing and examination, as has preceded.

Al-Farrā' said: "Kallā" in this place means: it was not fitting for the servant to be in this condition, but rather he should praise God for wealth and for poverty.

Then the Exalted moved from describing the evil of man's words to describing the evil of his deeds, and so He said: ﴿Nay, you do not honor the orphan﴾. The turn to direct address (al-iltifāt ilā al-khiṭāb) is for the purpose of reproach and censure, according to the recitation of the majority with the second-person form (al-fawqiyyah).

Al-Jumhūr recited "taḥāḍḍūna," "ta'kulūna," and "tuḥibbūna" with the second-person form (al-fawqiyyah) for address in them.

Abū 'Amr and Ya'qūb recited them with the third-person form (al-taḥtiyyah). The plural in these verbs is in view of the meaning of "al-insān," because what is meant by it is the category. That is: "Nay, you have deeds that are uglier than what has been mentioned, namely that you abandon honoring the orphan, so you eat his wealth and withhold from him the surplus of your own wealth."

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Qudāma ibn Maẓ'ūn, who was an orphan in the custody of Umayya ibn Khalaf.

﴿And you do not urge one another to feed the needy﴾. Al-Jumhūr recited "tuḥḍḍūna," from "ḥaddahu 'alā kadhā," meaning he incited him to it, and its object is omitted: that is, "you do not urge yourselves," or "none of you urges another to that, nor commands it, nor guides to it." The Kufans recited "tataḥāḍḍūna" with a fatḥa on the tā' and an alif after the ḥā', and its origin is "tataḥāḍḍūna," so one of the two tā's is dropped: that is, "none of you urges another."

Al-Kisā'ī in one of the transmissions from him, and al-Sulamī, recited "tuḥāḍḍūna" with a ḍamma on the tā', from al-ḥaḍḍ, which is urging. His words ﴿on the feeding of the needy﴾ are related to "tuḥḍḍūna." It is either a verbal noun (ism maṣdar), meaning "on feeding the needy," or a noun for the food, and it would then be with an elided modifier (ḥadhf muḍāf), meaning "on giving out the food of the needy," or "on giving the food of the needy."

﴿And you devour the inheritance﴾. Its origin is "al-wurāth," so the tā' was substituted for a ḍammed wāw, as in "tujāh" and "wijāh." What is meant by it is the wealth of orphans who inherit it from their relatives, and likewise the wealth of women. That is because they used not to give inheritance to women and children, and they would consume their wealth ﴿with greedy devouring﴾, meaning intense devouring. It was also said the meaning of "lamman" is gathering, from the saying: "lamamtu al-ṭa'ām," when you ate all of it.

Al-Ḥasan said: He eats his own share and the share of the orphan. Abū 'Ubayda said likewise.

The original meaning of "al-lamm" in Arabic speech is gathering. It is said: "lamamtu al-shay' alummuhu lamman," meaning I gathered it. From this is the saying: "lamma Allāh sha'athahu," meaning God gathered what had scattered of his affairs. From this is the verse of al-Nābigha:

"You are not one who would leave behind a brother whom you do not gather up, despite his disorder; which of men is refined?"

Al-Layth said: "al-lamm" is intense gathering, and from it come "ḥajar malmūm" (a gathered stone) and "katība malmūma" (a gathered army). The one who eats "yalummu al-tharīd," meaning he gathers the bread-and-broth and then eats it.

Mujāhid said: He lap it up (yasiffuhu saffan).

Ibn Zayd said: When he has consumed his own wealth, he gathers together the wealth of others and eats it, without considering what he has eaten of the foul and the good.

﴿And you love wealth with abundant love﴾, meaning intense love. "Al-jamm" is the abundant. It is said: "jamma al-mā' fī al-ḥawḍ," when the water increased and gathered. "Al-jamma" is the place where water gathers.

Then the Exalted repeated the deterrent and rebuke to them, and said: "Kallā," meaning this is not how your deeds should be.

Then the Exalted began anew, and said: ﴿When the earth is ground to powder, grinding upon grinding﴾. In this is a warning to them after the deterrent and rebuke. "Al-dakk" is breaking and crushing. The meaning here: it was shaken and moved with a movement after a movement.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Its mountains were crushed until they became level.

Al-Zajjāj said: That is, it was shaken and so some of it crushed others.

Al-Mubarrad said: That is, it was spread out and its elevation disappeared. He said: "al-dakk" is bringing down the elevated by flattening. The discussion of "al-dakk" has already preceded in the surah al-A'rāf and in the surah al-Aḥqāf. The meaning: it was crushed once after another. The accusative of the first "dakkan" is as a verbal noun emphasizing the verb, and the second "dakkan" is an emphasis of the first, so said Ibn 'Uṣfūr.

It is permissible that the accusative is as a circumstantial (ḥāl), meaning in the state of being crushed time after time, as one says: "I taught him arithmetic chapter by chapter (bāban bāban), and I taught him the script letter by letter (ḥarfan ḥarfan)." The meaning: He repeated the crushing upon it until it became scattered dust (habā'an munbaththan).

﴿And your Lord comes﴾, meaning His command and His decree comes, and His signs appear. It was also said the meaning is: the doubts on that day cease, and the realities become manifest and necessary, as doubt vanishes upon the arrival of the thing that was being doubted. It was also said: the subjugation of your Lord, His authority, and His sole control of the command and governance comes, without giving anyone of His servants any part of that. ﴿And the angels, rank upon rank﴾. The accusative of "ṣaffan ṣaffan" is as a circumstantial: that is, "lined up," or "possessors of rows."

'Aṭā' said: He means the rows of angels, and the people of each heaven are a separate row.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The people of each heaven, when they descend on the Day of Resurrection, will be a row encircling the earth and those upon it, so they will be seven rows.

﴿And Hell will be brought on that day﴾. "Yawma'idhin" is in the accusative governed by "jī'a." The one standing in place of the subject is "bi-Jahannam." Makkī permitted that "yawma'idhin" be the one standing in place of the subject, but that is not right.

Al-Wāḥidī said: A group of the exegetes said: It will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, bridled with seventy thousand bridles, with each bridle having seventy thousand angels dragging it, until it is placed on the left side of the Throne. No angel brought near, nor prophet sent, will remain without falling to his knees, saying: "O Lord, myself! myself!"

This which he transmitted from a group of exegetes will come, God willing, traced back to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

﴿On that day man will remember﴾. "Yawma'idhin" here is a substitute for the "yawma'idhin" preceding it, meaning: on the day Hell is brought, man will remember.

That is, he will take admonition, recall what he neglected, and regret what he sent ahead of himself in the world of disbelief and sins.

It was also said that the second "yawma'idhin" is a substitute for the phrase "idhā dukkat," and that the governing element for both is His words "yatadhakkaru al-insān."

﴿But how will the remembrance benefit him?﴾, meaning from where will he have remembrance and admonition? It was also said it is with an elided modifier: that is, from where will he have the benefit of the remembrance?

Al-Zajjāj said: He shows repentance, but from where is repentance?

﴿He will say, "Would that I had sent ahead for my life!"﴾ The sentence is a resumptive answer to an implied question, as if it was said: What will man say? It is also permissible that it is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) for His words "yatadhakkaru." The meaning: he wishes that he had sent ahead good and righteous deeds. The "lām" in "li-ḥayātī" means "for the sake of my life." What is meant is the life of the Hereafter, for it is the life in reality, because it is everlasting and not cut off.

It was also said that the "lām" means "in," and what is meant is the life of this world: that is, "Would that I had sent ahead righteous deeds during my life in the world, so that I might benefit from them this day." The first is preferable.

Al-Ḥasan said: By God, he knew that he had encountered a long life in which there is no death.

﴿So on that day none will punish as He punishes﴾, meaning on the day when the time of what has been mentioned of these conditions is, none will punish as God punishes. ﴿Nor will anyone bind as He binds﴾, or: none other than Him will undertake the punishment of God and His binding, since the whole matter belongs to Him. The two pronouns in both interpretations, in "'adhābihi" and "wathāqihi," refer to God, the Mighty and Majestic. This is according to the recitation of the majority, "yu'adhdhibu" and "yūthiqu," both in the active voice.

Al-Kisā'ī recited both in the passive voice, so the two pronouns refer back to man: that is, none will be punished with the punishment of that man, and none will be bound with his binding. "Al-insān" here means the disbeliever: that is, none who is not a disbeliever will be punished with the punishment of the disbeliever. It was also said it means Iblīs, and it was said it means Ubayy ibn Khalaf.

Al-Farrā' said: The meaning is that none will punish with the punishment of this specific disbeliever, nor bind with chains and shackles as he is bound, because of his extreme disbelief and obstinacy.

It was also said the meaning is: none will be punished in his place, and none will be bound in his place, so no ransom will be taken from him. This is like His words: ﴿And no bearer of burden shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'ām: 164]. "Al-'adhāb" is with the meaning of the punishing, and "al-wathāq" with the meaning of the binding.

Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred the recitation of al-Kisā'ī. He said: The pronoun in both places would be the pronoun of the disbeliever, since it is known that none punishes as God punishes.

Abū 'Alī al-Fārisī said: It is permissible that the pronoun refers to the disbeliever according to the recitation of the majority: that is, none punishes anyone as this disbeliever is punished.

When the Exalted finished relating the conditions of the wretched, He mentioned some conditions of the blessed, and so He said: ﴿O soul at peace﴾. "Al-muṭma'innah" is the one who is tranquil and certain in faith and in the oneness of God, who has reached the coolness of certainty (thalj al-yaqīn), such that no doubt mixes with it and no suspicion afflicts it.

Al-Ḥasan said: She is the believer who is certain.

Mujāhid said: She is the one content with God's decree, who knows that what missed her would never have been destined to reach her, and that what reached her would never have been destined to miss her.

Muqātil said: She is the safe and reassured one.

Ibn Kaysan said: "The tranquil soul" (al-mutma'innah) is the one at peace through the remembrance of God. It was also said: "the sincere one" (al-mukhlisah). Ibn Zayd said: it is called "the tranquil" because it was given the good news of Paradise at death and at the Resurrection.

﴿Return to your Lord﴾: that is, return to God, well-pleased with the reward He has given you, and well-pleasing in His sight. It was also said: return to His promise; and it was said: return to His command.

ʿIkrimah and ʿAta' said: the meaning of ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ is: return to your body in which you were. Ibn Jarir chose this view, and what supports it is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, "fa-odkhuli fi ʿabdi" (in the singular). The first view is preferable.

﴿Enter among My servants﴾: that is, among the company of My righteous servants; be one of them and join their ranks.

﴿And enter My Paradise﴾ along with them. It was said that she will be told "Return to your Lord" when she departs from this world, and she will be told "Enter among My servants and enter My Paradise" on the Day of Resurrection. The verse is meant in its general sense for every tranquil soul, and its revelation concerning a specific person does not preclude this; the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿eating (the inheritance) greedily (aklan lamma)﴾, that he said: "sweeping (safF)". And regarding His words ﴿love of wealth, immensely (hubban jamma)﴾, he said: "intensely." Ibn Jarir related from him also: ﴿aklan lamma﴾, he said: "intensely."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, regarding His words ﴿when the earth is leveled, leveled and leveled (dakkan dakka)﴾, that he said: "its shaking."

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "On that Day Hell will be brought forth, having seventy thousand bridles, with every bridle seventy thousand angels pulling it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿and how can he have the remembrance (wa-anna lahu al-dhikra)﴾ that he said: "And how could he?" Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His words ﴿on that Day none will punish as He punishes﴾ the verse, he said: "None will punish with the punishment of God, and none will bind with the bond of God."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from him also, regarding His words ﴿O tranquil soul﴾, he said: "the believing soul." ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ means: to your body.

He said: This verse was revealed while Abu Bakr was sitting, and he said: "O Messenger of God, how beautiful this is!" He said: "As for her, she will be told this."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nuʿaym in al-Hilyah related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr something similar, as a mursal report.

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul related something similar from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿O tranquil soul﴾ that it means "the one who affirms (the truth)."

Ibn Jarir related from him also regarding the verse that he said: "Souls will be returned to bodies on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding His words ﴿Return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ that he said: "with what she was given of reward, being well-pleased with her by her deeds." ﴿Enter among My servants﴾ means: the believers.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he said: Ibn ʿAbbas died at al-Ta'if, and a bird came, of a form not seen before, and entered his bier, and then it was not seen coming out of it. When he was buried, this verse was recited at the edge of the grave, and we do not know who recited it: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing, enter among My servants, and enter My Paradise.﴾

Abu Nuʿaym in al-Dala'il related something similar from ʿIkrimah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 89, verses 15–30 (part 1 of 2):

When the Exalted mentioned that He is ever watchful (bi-l-mirsad), He mentioned what indicates the variation in His servants' conditions upon receiving good and upon receiving evil, and that the object of their gaze and the greatest of their aims is this world. So He said: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him﴾, meaning He tries and examines him with blessings, ﴿and honors him and bestows favor upon him﴾, meaning He honors him with wealth and widens his provision. ﴿Then he says, "My Lord has honored me,"﴾ rejoicing in what he has attained and delighted in what he has been given, not thankful to God for it, and not considering that this is a trial from his Lord, a test of his state and a disclosure of what he harbors of patience, impatience, gratitude for the blessing, or ingratitude for it. The "mā" in His words "idhā mā" is superfluous (zā'idah). His words ﴿and honors him and bestows favor upon him﴾ are an explanation of the "testing." The meaning of "akramanī" is: He has favored me with the wealth He has given me and lavished blessings upon me, because I deserve it more and because I am its appropriate recipient. "Al-insān" is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "fa-yaqūlu rabbī akramanī." The "fa" entered into it because "amma" (as for) carries the sense of a conditional. The adverbial phrase placed between the subject and the predicate, although it precedes in wording, is delayed in meaning. That is: "As for man, then he says, 'My Lord has honored me,' at the time of his being tested with favors."

Al-Kalbi said: "al-Insān" is the disbeliever, Ubayy ibn Khalaf.

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Umayya ibn Khalaf. It was also said it was revealed concerning Utba ibn Rabi'a and Abu Hudhayfa ibn al-Mughira.

﴿But as for when He tests him﴾, meaning He examines him and treats him as one who is being examined, ﴿and so restricts his provision for him﴾, meaning He constricts it and does not widen it for him nor extends it to him. ﴿Then he says, "My Lord has humiliated me,"﴾ meaning He has assigned him humiliation. This is the attribute of the disbeliever who does not believe in the Resurrection, for to him there is no honor except the world and the widening of its enjoyments, and there is no humiliation to him except losing them and failing to reach what he desires of its adornments. As for the believer, honor for him is that God honors him by his obedience and enables him to perform the works of the Hereafter. It is possible that "al-insān" is intended in a general sense, because of his lack of certainty that what came to him of good in this world and what befell him of evil are nothing but a test and an examination, and that the whole world is not worth, in the sight of God, the wing of a mosquito. Had it been worth the wing of a mosquito, He would not have given the disbeliever a single sip of water from it.

Nāfi' recited with the ya' (the final long vowel) affirmed in "akramanī" and "ahānanī" when connected, and omitted them when pausing. Ibn Kathīr, in the transmission of al-Bazzī from him, and Ibn Muḥaysin, and Ya'qūb recited with both affirmed, both in connection and in pause. The rest recited with both omitted in connection and in pause, following the orthography of the Muṣḥaf (the written codex) and for conformity with the ends of verses (ru'ūs al-āy). The original form is with them affirmed, since it is a noun (ism). Among the omission is the poet's verse:

"And from an enemy whose hidden rancor is apparent, when I stand before him, he disowned me (ankaranī)."

That is, "ankaranī" (he disowned me).

Al-Jumhūr recited "fa-qadara" with the light form (takhfīf), and Ibn 'Āmir recited it with the doubled form (tashdīd), and both are dialects.

Al-Ḥaramayn (Ibn Kathīr and Nāfi') and Abū 'Amr recited "rabbī" with a fatḥa on the ya' in both places, and the rest recited it with sukūn.

His words "kallā" (no indeed) are a deterrent to man who said what he said in both states, and a rebuke to him. For God, the Exalted, may widen provision and extend blessings to a person, not as a sign of his honor, and He may constrict it for him, not as a sign of his humiliation, but for testing and examination, as has preceded.

Al-Farrā' said: "Kallā" in this place means: it was not fitting for the servant to be in this condition, but rather he should praise God for wealth and for poverty.
